text: I used about 90 feet of cat-6 cable to connect this.  Some of the cable is cat-6a, connected to cat-6 in the middle, so cat-6 is the standard I can count on.  It works for 4k@30, but not 4k@60 and not 3d.  I put cables in the wall when the room was being built, and didn't know that 50' HDMI cables that say they work don't always.  So I'm upset, but this helped fix the problem because I ran ethernet to both locations and a few extra cables too.  If this did 3d, I would be 100% happy.  Since it doesn't, I may have to put the blu-ray player up with the projector and figure out a way to return the audio instead of using this for it.  But this will work for the cable box and computer that are also connected.  So, in summary, if you want 3d and have Cat-6 cable, this doesn't work.  If 4k@30 is enough without 3d, then this is what you need and it works great!  In case you are curious, I tested using two HDMI switches too, and the 4k@30 survived going through both switches and this pair too!

I have a GeForce 750Ti and I broke the HDMI output on it.  I bought this because I found that my video card can provide audio via the DVI output.  This is a good product.  There is one issue that I find when playing video.  There is a hangup/buzzing that occurs periodically and in close succession.  It isn't something most folks would put up with.  I cannot say it is caused by the cable.  It may be my card.  I obviously did something to make the HDMI port stop working and it is reasonable to question if that impacted the card overall.

Smart watches have gotten more popular with the release of the Apple watch. They tend to have a standard set of functions, such as access to instant messaging, email, time, alarms and a lot more, typically tied to your phone. Not all smart watches are alike, though, and offer different sets of functions, better connectivity and other various differences from one another. This particular smart watch offers the mainline set of functions, setting itself apart through the user interface which is more polished and clean than most others with which I have worked. That said, I have a couple of quibbles with it, leaving room for a little improvement.

This is a standard-sized watch with a rubber wristband that can actually fit a larger wrist like mine. I have trouble finding watches and watch bands that fit me, so the fact that this one fits me is a pleasant surprise.

Powering it on, the user is immediately greeted with a complex and fairly complete visual menu system with tiles for every function available to the user. This is a standard presentation for a smartwatch, but this one looks a bit more polished and clean than the others I have seen. Switching to other menu screens just requires a swipe gesture, as to be expected. I have big hands, and this means that, for me, using a stylus makes working with this watch a lot easier. This is not the fault of the watch but a reality of working with a small device.

My first issue with this watch came when I paired it to my phone. The date and time on the watch were off, so I expected that it would grab the time from my iPhone when I paired it. It did not. Instead, I had to dig for the clock application and manually set the time. I dislike this and think that having it set itself when it is paired is much more accurate and cuts effort on the part of the user. For Android users, there is an application to allow for syncing up the time, date and more, but iOS users are out of luck for now. To the manufacturer's credit this is made clear on the product listing so this is not a surprise. Regardless, I am of the opinion that the watch should fetch the time, not rely on being sent the time. In the grand scheme of things, though, this is an annoyance, not a deal breaker.

There is a fairly comprehensive list of functions provided by this watch in addition to time/date and phone answer. Through the menus the user has access to call logs and function, Bluetooth functions, a remote finder function, a pedometer, a sleep monitor, a reminder function to get up and move on occasion, calendar and clock functions, audio functions, video functions and a few more.

One of the interesting functions that this watch offers is a camera. So, I tried to use it and it complained that there was no memory card available. Reading through the limited documentation included, I was unable to find anything about a memory card. I finally noticed that the back of the watch has a small groove where it can be popped off, and when I removed the back I found the battery which is removable (replaceable - another pleasant surprise). Under the battery is a slot for a micro SD card.

Adding a memory card comes with a big catch. It requires removing the battery to get at the holder which in turn clears the clock and resets it to midnight 01-01-2015. So, adding the memory card requires me to set the time again. And again if I remove the card.

Although I think the time sync functions of this watch are lacking, it is otherwise a good smartwatch. The interface is professional and polished and the whole provides access to a large number of useful functions. It's priced well too. Overall, this is a solid offering worth a look if you are wanting a smartwatch.

The Belkin Miracast Video Adapter works well if the correct equipment is available, but doesn't work at all if you are using a noncompliant smartphone or television.  I first thought my two year old Vizio television would not work because it has no USB port, but after ordering a new set, realized that the USB could be utilized from an outside source.  After trying several times to ate my Razr to the Belkin, I realized that the connection was unobtainable because the phone is not operating on the correct system.  I then enlisted a friend with a compatible phone and we were able to make the connection very quickly, then watched gleefully on the Vizio.  For a smartphone with Miracast capability, this works well and should be considered.  Since technology changes rapidly, as do our phones, I would not hesitate to use this if it fits into your budget.  When I replace my smartphone in the next few months, I will certainly verify on the Belkin website that the new purchase is compatible because it is an outstanding option for viewing images and listening to audio on a big screen.  I have been satisfied with my other Belkin products and find them to be a reliable company.  If your set has an HDMI port which isn't easy to access, this device also includes an extender which has worked well for my set.  Otherwise, I would not have been able to plug in the USB cable because of its position.

This new AmazonBasics iPad Smart Case with Auto wake and sleep will fit the new iPad Air 2 tablets. It has a hard back and a soft front. The front can be wrapped around and inserted in the middle of the back and used as a stand. For the price point, this has all the cutouts in the right place and you won't have to remove the case to charge it, insert audio into it or take photos. I was concerned about the camera portion but when I tested it, it worked just fine. One thing I found interesting, is that inside the box was a sticker to prevent mold. First time seeing that in a box, but living in Florida, it is a great idea.

I do still plan to use this for audiobook listening when I'm doing loud things, like showering (big plus it's waterproof) but I've been traveling and haven't had time to set it up and try it.

We finally got around to using this speaker last night for our NYE pregaming at my house. We played old school hip hop and rocked it for a few hours. The bass was a little disappointing, but I think it proved it will be perfect for my audiobooks, even if it's not ideal for music.

I will start by saying we have high speed internet, with extenders, so speed of tablet can not be from our internet. All other devices work great. The tablet comes with charging cable & plug. Charges well. It is a good portable size. I have been using for several days. I have it set up with all apps I will use. Have streamed some programs, it buffers from time to time. I have listened to audiobooks, no issues. Apps work fine, but are a little slow. Same with reviewing email. I mostly use my smartphone for that, but wanted to try it in different ways prior to reviewing. It is great, no. It is good, yes. That being said, it seems like a good value for the price ($59.99 at time of review). If you spent several hundred dollars, it wouldn’t be acceptable, but for the price, it seems like a good value. I will say, it was super slow the first use, while setting up. I fully charged it before doing so, though it had a decent charge upon arrival. After the first use, it did seem a bit faster, not sure why that would be. If your expectation, is lightning fast, I would pass. I think it would be food for the younger set or for travel, if you don’t want to take your expensive electronics. It is a decent tablet, just not the fastest. Each person will have decide if it will be right for them, based on budget & expectations. For me, it will get used regularly.

If you want a 10" tablet for reading books and watching videos/TV shows/movies and can't afford more money than this (price regularly drops to $100), then this is good product choice. Performance is fine for e-books and videos, but sometimes sluggish for intense game playing, photo/video editing or even text editing. The SD card slot lets you store lots of TV shows and movies and use the main memory for apps (which often work poorly if stored on the SD card). Kindle e-books sometimes work much better on the Fire tablets than on ipads or Android tablets, especially if the books have embedded audio or video. The user interface revolves around the books and videos that you bought from Amazon. With a considerable amount of work, you may be able to replace the user interface with a more standard Android launcher that focuses on your apps and files. Realistically, the performance of this tablet clunky enough that I don't recommend it unless you are mostly using it for e-books and videos, so maybe changing the user interface is not worth the effort.

You should also ask yourself if you are using the tablet for mostly e-books and videos, do you really need a 10 inch screen? The 8 inch Kindle Fire tablet has similar performance and a much lower price and is also lighter weight and less bulky, making it easier to use in many situations.

What I like about this camera is that I can use this for any room in my house. For us, I decided to use it in the living room. First, because I can pan it down a bit more than some others so I can see more of the floor where my pets are.
It's very easy to set up. Downloaded the app and registered, plugged it in, set up our WiFi, and it was ready to go.
It did take me a little looking to find where to insert the SD card. (in front bubble part at the bottom)
The only problem I had was when I hit the record button on the app. Worked fine until I closed the app. Then it came up with a "failed" notification that popped up.
When I try to look back at video it says "hmm...there's no video in this time".
So right now I can only use this in real time until I can talk with a tech to figure out what is wrong. Or figure this out myself. I might format the SD card and try setting it all up again.
But, I like the picture quality in daytime and in night vision. Audio is a little delayed but works fine.
The panning and zoom function are great too.

This is a very cute and small designed projector. It comes with a remote to operate.  It has HDMI, AUX audio, video ports as well, no optical port and Zoom, keystone adjustment features. When it comes to picture quality it is 720P native and 1080P supported, so the picture won't look super clear if you are used for 1080P. Otherwise everything else is good with the given price for this item.

Very impressed with this speaker. I play a lot of dubstep and the bass is pretty good wuality. Not as loud as I’d like it to be but I really struggle with finding good portable speakers with good bass and this is the best I’ve found so far.
I'm a bass crazy lover but this works well

I like the construction, the self stand and the looks of the cover. What I don't like and would love to fix is that I am somewhat hard of hearing and if I close the cover over the touch screen, I can barely hear the narrator of my Audible book.
I would use ear buds but they all seem to be geared to heavy bass, which I don't need.

I like these headphones for their quality and price. I have these and Samsung Galaxy buds. The Galaxy buds win in terms of convenience and features due to me having a Galaxy phone, but the X5 wins in terms of volume and bass. I like to listen to music with bass and the Galaxy buds just don't have that at all, plus noise cancelling is gimmicky on the buds and eventually I have to up the volume to truly drown out all noise, which is easier to do with the X5. Both headphones shine in different respects. When it comes to interacting with my phone I prefer the features provided by Galaxy buds, but when it comes to listening to music and comfort then I prefer the X5, plus the X5 is way more economical. The mic on both for calls were not impressive. They work well enough in a quiet room but when I'm in my car I have to turn off my AC to use them (the AC isn't blowing on my face, they just really pick up on the air blowing around in general). Overall I don't think most people will be disappointed with this purchase.

First, getting the ear fit right is awkward. None of the earfits really secure them well. These are bigger than ‘buds’. When you have them fitted to your ear in a least worse choice sort of way, the fidelity and most especially the bass is fantastic … as good as I’ve ever heard from such a compact package. But … they are too big/heavy for use on the treadmill. I can’t keep them in my skull.

For non-workout use, these are likely the best full fidelity you’ll find. The ‘earbud for workout’ application just isn’t working for me. If you’re not looking for active wear, these are really superb commuter 'super-buds'

We are a family of noise cancelling headphones. What I loved about these phones:
1. Great bass and really enjoyable experience whether music or audible books;
2. I have a big head, they fit comfortably as the design allows for a great level of flex on how the ear phones fit on your head;
3. The functional buttons are on both sides! And they are big enough that you can without pressing the wrong button. Too many times, the high end phones cram all the buttons on one side - why?
4. The noise cancelling works! We tested with our air conditioner on - it’s a rattler. Totally stripped out that noise and still enjoyed listening to my music. Great to use on TV with Bluetooth. Used it whilst I was walking in my concrete jungle environment. Totally enjoyed listening to audible books.
5. Comes with a beautiful case and add ons for airplanes, or connector if you don’t want to use the Bluetooth functionality. Bluetooth was easy to connect to our various Bluetooth devices: android and Apple.

These are great inexpensive ear buds.  My only complaint would be  lack of bass in the music.  Other than that, these are a good low-cost selection for some wireless buds.  I use mine every day at work.

The OontZ Angle 3 PLUS speaker has incredible battery life, pretty good bass, somewhat muddy mid range and okay highs (if you use the right app with a good equalizer). I found playing straight from the phone's built in apps wasn't so great but I downloaded another app with powerful settings and controls that bring out the best of this speaker. The OontZ Angle 3 PLUS has two speakers and 10 watts of power. There's a passive bass radiator. I never really thought those added much. All in all it's a decent speaker that kicks up my shower and shaving time. I got this on a Lightning Deal for a nice discount. I would not pay the full asking price.

The primary purpose of this speaker is to have something louder than my phone in the shower, around the pool, or at the beach. For the price, it is a good solution.

Battery life and portability appear excellent. Very easy to connect and it can get fairly loud without significant distortion. In terms of tonal quality it’s not bad. Very mid-range heavy. I typically find myself using an in-app EQ to boost the highs to get more clarity. It’s a small speaker so don’t expect any bass. At the beach with constant ambient noise, this works.

Biggest drawback is poor Bluetooth reception. 10-15ft and it starts dropping out badly and it’s even worse if your body is in between the phone and the speaker. I don’t have a big pool but i can’t be on one side with my iPhone 11Pro and have a clear, consistent connection to the speaker. If Bluetooth reception were stronger, this would be 5-stars for value. But again, for having a little music while sitting with a friend at the beach, it works well enough.

For the price, I’d recommend it as a good value.

This radio can be recharged via built-in solar panel (which takes twenty hours or more) or by built-in hand crank, or by the mini USB port. There's a full-size USB port for using the radio's built-in battery to recharge devices. It also can be powered by three AAA batteries (which aren't included).

The speaker is just about ideal for spoken messages like weather alerts, but not high fidelity for music. Forget about bass response -- there isn't any to speak of.

The three bands are FM, AM, and NOAA. There's also an "alert" setting, which I assume means the radio will wake up and start broadcasting when it detects the NOAA weather alert signals. The instructions don't mention this.

The AM band volume is a little low compared to FM and NOAA bands. There's no headphone jack. No text alerts. It's not a digital, so tuning with the wheel can be a bit finicky. The telescoping rod antenna is okay, but you probably have had similar experience that those can be the first thing to break, so it's a good idea to handle that with some care. It also has a built-in flashlight.

Since it's basically an analog radio and not programmable and doesn't have text message alerts, if you live in a severe weather-prone area, this might not be the weather radio you want as your primary radio. But with all the recharge options it might be one to consider as a backup or for carrying camping.

I wanted a smaller device as a backup to my iPad2, so I bought this secondhand. It was easy to navigate around the contents. I added a N2A(Nook to Android) 32GB microSD card so I can also access android apps and have more storage. Amazon has the best price for that and after installing the card, I can get more out of this device. It was a little frustrating at first to navigate around the android OS but it has been worth it. Sometimes my iPad2 is too large to carry around, and the Nook Color easily slips inside my purse. I am using this mainly as an ereader and note taker. Maybe later I might install some free games. Putting on an antiglare screen helped a lot for when I am in bright light settings. The color and clarity of the content is really nice. I gave this only 4 stars because I think the OS could still use some tweaking. Overall I am pleased.

There are things that I like and dislike about this computer. Much of it is simply personal preference over the actual computer.

Pros:

- The colors of the keyboard are really cool
-the picture color is amazing. I watch videos and tv shows on it often because I enjoy the clarity of the picture

Cons:

- smaller screen (which I know) but there is not a side number keyboard which I really prefer.

I don't use this computer for gaming purposes. I am a teacher and I use it for classroom at home on the weekends. I would buy this computer again... except for the cost. If it was about $900.00 cheaper. Compared to other laptops that I have, I see no difference over all in this computer and others. It just simply isn't worth the cost in my opinion. However, that is a personal reason and I will not take off from the review for that.

SO this has an IPS monitor which gives you higher definition and clarity than an LED monitor. But also it uses more energy and these types of monitors are known for heating up and overheating which can cause premature failure. To further add to this issue, some genius put its heat fan pointed RIGHT at the front of the monitor. I've never seen this in a laptop and don't understand why they couldn't vent it out the side or even reposition the monitor slightly so they could vent the heat out the back. I'm really hoping that the heat blowing onto the monitor that's already known for heat issues isn't gonna be an issue. Within a few short minutes of regular browsing, its fan is blowing non-stop and the bottom part of the actual computer screen is getting hot because of the exhaust fan.

Other than the screen and heat issue, the laptop seems to be nicely made. It only took a couple of minutes to setup and streams videos/ surfs the net flawlessly when paired with my gigabit internet. It's not slow at all- loads programs quickly and loads web pages quickly.

I think it's a good computer overall and they're on the right track with this one. It looks really cool and runs great! The thing that I love about it's finish is it's not glossy- those always scratch up and look junky quickly. The finish on this one will stay looking great for years I'm sure!

Music clarity and Bluetooth connection are great.  However the controls suck.  Controlling ANC is the worst.  Have to remove headset everytime control's need adjusting.  I was very hopeful but they may get returned.
I use it next to my bed to see the time , is a small clock but with a lot of clarity

This is a fantastic IPS panel display that actually closely matches my laptop display in clarity, brightness and size/position. That makes it great for a quick "second screen" when I need to make a portable workstation on the go! Ideally, it should be possible to run the entire thing off a USB-C connection, so you don't need any additional power/hdmi/usb/etc connection. They advertise that this is possible.
However I was unable to get that to work. For some reason, my HP laptop, despite having a USB-C port, would not recognize this as a monitor. Neither would my phone which also supports display port over USB-C.
I needed to use the hdmi cable adapter, and then I was able to use the USB-C for power from my laptop. Interesting to note that if you want to use the display's touch screen capability, use the monitor in USB-C instead of the strictly powered one, and it will support full touch screen as well as power the unit. I was nervous when the single-cable setup didn't work that it would require all three plugs to be used in separate- power usb, usb for touch, and hdmi for video signal. 3 cables would have been too much and I'd just never use it. 2 cables are doable. I'd think a low powered unit such as a Raspberry Pi might require separate power since it likely can't supply enough power for the monitor, but the mini PC and laptop I tried it with seemed to do just fine running the monitor and using the same USB for touch-input support. I really wish it only required the single USB cable, however. I was unable to get that working no matter what I tried.
For what its worth, I'd give it 4 stars since it adds a touch enabled second screen to my laptop, and also makes my miniPC into a kiosk for interesting use at events. But I wish I could get it working with a single cable like it advertises. That would make it 5 stars.

I received this as a free review sample five months ago and have been using it for around four months. This is a rear view monitor only - not a dashcam - and it works far better than one of the combination rear monitors/dashcams that I have also used.

Since there are a large number of reviews that cover this in detail I am going to keep mine brief. Here is the single thing I do not like about it: the terrible documentation. On the other hand you can have this professionally installed for not a lot of money, which is the route that I took. If you are a do-it-yourselfer installing it right is less than an hour job (according to the tech who installed mine).

What I love is the clear visual behind me. The camera works in dark and low light, and the display has sufficient clarity and resolution to easily see what is behind you and estimate distances. If you were to purchase this as an option on a vehicle I shudder to think of the cost, but for less than one hundred fifty bucks professionally installed this is a bargain. And if you do install it yourself you can knock a C-note off that cost.

If you parallel park frequently this is a perfect way to make that easier. For rural driving this may not be a needed accessory, but for city use it's a convenience (and a safety feature as well.) Do note the information in the product specs too because they are clear about what this will and will not work with.

I gave this 4 stars I like it . Its very fast loading movies , picture clarity is awesome ! Your choices of programs are many , over all I think its a great system.As a mater of fact better then most that are out there.

I purchased this for my Samsung Galaxy Tab S4 10.1, which I just picked up off eBay. The install was fairly easy - I used Supershieldz before and while their smartphone protectors are far easier to install than these on account of the smaller size, the experience was highly comparable. In the end did have a couple tiny air bubbles - so small that they were only iridescent patches - which I could not work to the edges of the screen no matter how I tried. However, I just left the Galaxy Tab in a warm room overnight, and the next day, they were totally gone and have not yet returned, more than month later.

Responsiveness is indistinguishable from the base touchscreen. Clarity is, so far as I can tell, perfect. Very low friction, though it still picks up fingerprints. I really like that it comes with two protectors, just in case one breaks in the future. The fact that the screen had a couple (very) minor scratches near the edges did not affect the install whatsoever.

Install notes are unremarkable. I followed the instructions closely. Basically, you need a clean area with good light and low airflow. You should wear tight-knit clothing, like nylon or linen, instead of something fuzzy. If you have long hair, tie it back. Wear latex gloves. Make sure you have 15m or so to devote to the install. Remove the tablet from its case, clean the screen up, inspect it from multiple angles, then do the hinge-type install as instructed. I also recommend cleaning the screen protector with the included cloth before you start, even though it still has its protective film on it, as this will prevent it from transferring dust to the screen during the fitting process.

Getting it centered is still kind of tricky, especially on the 10.1" tablet, you have to be more careful that you would be with the phone or a smaller tablet. Just decide in the beginning that you are going to devote 15-20m to this install and take your time with it.

I now have Supershieldz on three devices, and would recommend.

I read the reviews but these seem to work fine for us. Got them for our granddaughter and she loves them. No issues so far. She is very careful though with them. We teach her to be careful with electronics. Good clarity and they fit snug.
Love the light that it blinks. Also came with an additional battery.

Here are my thoughts about Roku. Generally I like the product, but in setting it up I had some concerns.

PROS:
**Easy to set up
**Compact - it's so small it fits in one hand.
**Picture quality is pretty sharp depending upon the source. It is not HD quality but more like a decent DVD (though not Blu-Ray).
**A number of free channels available through Roku. You can add a lot of content. Since I'm an old movie buff, I added Pub a Hub (public domain movies) and Crackle (pretty bad recent movies but some good classics, like Easy Rider).
**Picture is big. I have a friend who has a projector that's five times as big as the Roku, and yet the projected image is the same size. That's impressive.

CONS:
**How much radiation does this device emit? In the fine print, the instruction booklet reads: "This equipment complies with FCC radiation exposure limits set forth for an uncontrolled environment. This equipment should be installed and operated with minimum distance 20CM between the RADIATOR AND YOUR BODY."
Hmm. I don't know about you, but it's hard not to sit pretty close to the projector. I used it in the bedroom and watched a movie on the ceiling. Of course I had to be close to it in order to put it at the right angle. How much radiation is the device emitting?

**Roku asks for your credit card information before you can use the device. When you set up an account, even if you don't want anything other than the free channels, they force you to put your credit card on file. The other privacy issue I object to is the way Roku allows you to connect to Facebook. In order for Roku to work, you were pretty much forced to allow Roku to access your information on Facebook at any time (even when you're logged out!) Not happy about this.

**In order to add some channels to the Roku network, you have to establish separate accounts. That means establishing one for Netflix, one for Amazon, etc, if you don't already have one. This means I'm sharing my account information with a number of companies I may or may not want to do business with. No doubt all this information will be shared among the video providers. That means a lot of spam will be coming my way in my email.

**Roku is geared toward convincing you to subscribe to as many streaming (pay on demand) services as possible. I'm not sure I would pay $300 for it, as it is very much a device aimed to getting you to subscribe to streaming channels. You can use it other ways, but Roku feels like a product sponsored by many vendors, as opposed to a stand-alone projector.

My conclusion? I recommend it with some reservations as noted above.

I ordered this lens and filter kit to go with my Samsung NX300 with the intent of expanding the capabilities of the camera without spending a fortune. I looked at several different kits before settling on this one, based on the price. I will admit to being a bit apprehensive about the cost in relation to the number of lenses and filters in the kit (presently this kit sells for less than $35 on Amazon as I write this) but my concern was ill-placed - this is a good kit.

I will start off by saying that I am not a professional photographer by any stretch of the imagination. I could be best described as an enthusiast who is trying to learn as I go.

I have experimented and played with many of the various components with this kit, starting with the 2.2x telephoto lens. This is a chunky item, which should be expected as it is a glass lens. It attached without issue to my 18mm-55mm OIS lens and I was able to use it almost immediately out of the box. It took me a little fiddling at first to get the focus just right as I am still learning with the camera but once I figured out the manual focus I was able to improve the zoom range with the telephoto lens in place. This, to me, is worth the cost of the kit. One thing I did notice, however, is that when the telescoping zoom is not fully extended on the regular lens, this lens adds a shadowy blackout area around the perimeter of the image that fades when the zoom is telescoped out.

My favorite component of this kit is the .43x wide-angle lens which works surprisingly well with the camera's included lens. It is another chunky item like the telephoto lens and it attaches easily as well. Even at closer ranges (15 feet or so) it allows the camera to capture appreciably more than the regular lens, without distortion. This is probably the one component I will use more than the others, and again this is an accessory that is worth the cost of the kit. This lens is not going to give the same quality result as a dedicated wide-angle lens but the price/quality tradeoff is worth it.

There are four close-up lenses in this kit that vary in strength. These are fun to play with though I did start to get a lot of edge distortion when using the strongest lens. This is not a problem as there are times when this kind of distortion is a good thing. I was able to get similar close-up shots - without distortion - with the Samsung lens but it required a lot more effort. Interestingly, one of these lenses had a smudge on it when I removed it from it's cellophane envelope. A quick wipe with a microfiber cloth did a fine job of cleaning the lens but this puzzled me - why was it smudged?

The wide-angle lens comes coupled with a macro lens that is absolutely astounding for close-up shots. I use this lens for taking pictures of pattern weaves, close-ups of surfaces, animal fur and other interesting subjects (the knee of my denim jeans makes a really interesting background shot). It works even a little better than the close-up lenses and is likely going to be the only lens I use for when I need a really detailed close-in shot of something. Though this lens outperforms the close-up magnifying lenses it requires decoupling from the wide-angle lens before it can be used and this is a minor hassle.

The kit includes a UV filter, a CPL filter and a FL-D filter. I used the CPL filter while experimenting and the result was minorly disappointing but I figured that was due to unrealistic expectations. It did tweak the color profile just a little but not dramatically like I had hoped. The FL-D filter was another story and gave the whole picture a completely different color profile. It is designed for use with fluorescent lighting (which means it should be used a lot when indoors) so when it is used with incandescent lighting it give a very eerie and unusual hue to pictures. With my lens I can adjust for fluorescent lighting electronically so this isn't a lens I necessarily need but I still like to mess with it. I have not tried the UV filter.

The cleaning kit is an important item in the kit, for removing dirt and smudges from the various lenses without using a harsh cloth. It's very basic but is a fine start - cleaning spray, cotton swabs, a microfiber cloth and a squeeze duster for puffing away particles when a full cleaning is not needed.

This kit includes a couple of other miscellaneous items as well, including a miniature tripod for a desk mount and a 6-compartment memory card storage case. These are nice-to-have extras, though I confess I am thoroughly unimpressed with the tripod which is a flexible bendy-leg tripod that does not retain the position in which it is set when supporting the camera, so it really is of little use. I continue to mess with the tripod, though, as I am sure I can get it to work in certain scenarios.

The main negative I encountered so far was actually the manner in which the kit was packaged and shipped to me. Everything was in a large plastic envelope bag with no padding at all. What would prevent the items in the kit from being crushed in such a shipment? Fortunately, all items were individually wrapped in small and sturdy cardboard boxes and one of those boxes was actually slightly crushed though there was no damage to the merchandise inside. Something like this should be shipped in a larger corrugated box, to better protect everything.

If you have a Samsung camera for which this kit is compatible, this is a very good kit to extend the capability of the camera without breaking the bank. The various lenses add range and effects, the filters are nice to have on hand and the extras are icing on the cake. At the current pricing, this is a very good deal.
Installed easily on the back of the camera and it appears to be able to do the job for which it was made.  No interference or distortion with the viewing area.
Surprising power with limited distortion.  Excellent for travel.

After using a number of screen protectors on various devices, this product is about par for the course. No distortion, and a nice look. Finger sliding is important to me, and this one has just the right amount of slip. If you've never applied a screen protector, go to youtube and watch a quick video, and remember to work in a dust free area!

Quality of build is evident in the Canon SX260 HS. Buttons and levers appear to be solid in both function and design; audible shutter activation is crisp and professional. The ability to set the F Stop, Shutter Speed and ISO manually, other than using the Auto setting is what makes this camera very special. The CMOS sensor adds to the total package, delivering crisp, professional photos. Images taken with the long zoom lens, despite it's 20X capabilities and being hand-held, were devoid of any distortion and held a high degree of resolution.

Cons: Battery life appeared notably short, perhaps due to using the zoom and GPS feature often. This has yet to be confirmed.
The location of the pop-up flash is where one would normally place an index finger over the top of the camera.
A conscious effort must be made to not interfere with the flash mechanism when using this camera.

I really needed one of these for my desktop during this time of teleconferencing for work and school. I wouldn't say it's incredible quality, a selfie camera on a modern flagship phone will have better, but it is absolutely usable for zoom meetings, skype calls, and real time streaming, and allows me to use the comfort of my desk and dual-monitor PC setup.
As you can see in the image, the view is rather wide, which comes with a bit of barrel distortion (look at the wall curve where it hits the ceiling- I promise this is straight in real life!). It's not a fish eye distortion, but it's slight and noticeable on straight edges. It has an LED indicator that comes on to tell you it has power, and then another light that comes on to tell you when it is active. I like this, because you have a visual indicator that your camera is on so that you won't have to worry about covering it for hackers or things like that. There is a mic but personally I like using an external mic that is closer to my mouth. The mic is OK on this, and definitely useful if you don't have one already. All in all, it is very functional and a major upgrade over my XP-era VGA resolution webcam from forever ago. Just don't expect it to be amazing. It's a good value for the price.

We have a minivan with a DVD entertainment system pre-installed. It predates the HDMI standard, so there are just RCA analog inputs in the back of the van. Since DVDs are pretty much obsolete, using this adapter we are able to plug in a laptop, raspberry pi or other digital video player to the car's system. I like that it is powered by USB, it is a convenient source of power especially when you don't have access to outlets (like in a car!). But you have to be careful about ground loop feedback. When powering it off a laptop, and the laptop is charging in the car, it can create either an audible hum and/or visual static distortion pattern on the video feed. This is common in DC circuits that share ground when working with analog equipment, unfortunately. I'm not sure if there's much that can be done about it other than try to run off batteries as often as possible (with this converter attached to a USB battery bank, the laptop on its own power, and the car running its own 12v DC). I have an older similar product looks almost identical that does the same thing so I'm guessing that's just a side effect of working with RCA inputs instead of digital ones.

I bought my example of this fisheye lens from ebay for the EOS mount. I use this on a 1.6x crop and I have also used it on a full frame camera as well. It's not good below f11, but it is good at f16. Ken Rockwell mentions this in his review of this lens. With this lens its best to increase ISO even at the expense of image noise rather than open up the aperture beyond f8. I have tried to use this lens at f2.8 in low light on a 1.6x crop camera and it just does not look good. Not only is there a large loss of sharpness but for some reason the image becomes more orange on my example. I should mention that with my ebay example the coating on the front element wasn't even, so it's possible that it might be from that.

The lens cap on mine doesn't stay on do to a broken tab, which can be annoying since it's specific to the lens.

I think this lens is a good deal, if it can be had for cheap. I'm not sure I would buy another one if I lost mine at the current prices that this lens goes for though. The primary reason would be because a fisheye lens has limited use do to barrel distortion, I'd rather put that money towards a rectilinear wide angle.

According to my husband, a former Boy Scout, camping aficionado and Nature lover, Bushnell makes excellent products. These binoculars live up to that reputation - they are well made, powerful in range (10x), and provide crystal clear views. Additionally, it's compact and thus easier to pack than our current pair from Barska. It has twist up eye cups, an adjustable bridge (so that they can rest comfortably on the nose and reduce eye strain) and a rubber casing that makes it easy to hold and grip. Best of all, these are waterproof (the instructions say you can immerse them in water and no damage to the insides will occur) and fog proof. We have not yet tested the waterproof claim but will update this review when we do. Clearly, the product is geared toward the serious nature enthusiast/hunter/explorer type. It comes with a strap, lens cap, and stylish carrying bag.

However, there is one problem - if you have a narrow face (as my husband does), you have to press the tubes very close together in order for it to sit comfortably on the bridge of your nose. Unfortunately, you can't do this without distorting your field of vision. As a result you're forced to spread it wider just to correct the distortion, at the cost of not having it feel 100% comfortable on your face.

Except for this issue, this is an excellent product that I can recommend with no reservation.

I played with Sony's HDR-AS30V and its accessories for a few hours, then took it with me (in its optional camcorder case) to videotape, and take photos for, a Christmas party. This is a nice little video camera as long as you are clear on what it's going to be used for. It's really not a replacement for a digital camera.

First, the accessories: Sony was kind enough to send me the camcorder cradle, wrist band mount, head band mount, and tripod angle mount to test with the HDR-AS30V, along with a package of the pretty essential anti-fog sheets. The video camera itself comes with a waterproof casing for underwater filming. The camera sits inside this case, but you can take it out to put it in the camcorder cradle instead (which is not waterproof, of course). In its waterproof casing, the video camera mounts well on any of the mounts. I tested the wrist mount on my chiweenie puppy (7 lbs.) but he didn't like it very much and it rolled around. On me, it's fine, also, but I don't do anything that would warrant my using it. The head mount has a wide band that fit to my head securely, but I don't do things with a helmet on so I couldn't test how it works for that.

Before I left for the Christmas party, I charged up the battery and replaced the 8GB SDHC card that came with my video camera with a 32GB one. I spent about half an hour with the video camera in Interval/5-second mode snapping photos and about 45 minutes non-stop videotaping activity. I really wasn't happy with the quality of the photos, however. I thought I had set the camera to its highest quality mode, but apparently I had not. I wound up with a lower-resolution appearance to the photos that really don't look all that good even onscreen. Another thing I did not like is the fisheye-like distortion at the edges, warped-looking (bent) walls and doors, and an odd color cast. Like I said, this camera is not a replacement for a digital camera.

What the HDR-AS30V shines at, though, is precisely what it's made for: rapid action shots from the perspective of the wearer. The video camera has good stability and the fisheye effect enhances the (for lack of a better word) intimacy of the action shots. The GPS capability and log is a really geeky thing that could even have some diagnostic utility for sports people. All in all, it's a lot of capability in a very tiny package that won't weigh or slow you down.

To be honest, I'm not likely to do much in the realm of action shots. I did find the camcorder case to be very lightweight and easy to use over several hours of time without fatigue. The battery held up during that time, and so did the 32GB storage. Extra batteries can be purchased cheaply, so you can always be ready to go. When I got back home from my party, it was just a matter of plugging in the USB cable into my computer and importing all my photos and movies using the PlayMemories software. I wouldn't give up Photoshop for PlayMemories, but it serves the purpose of importation well enough.

I think what I enjoy the most with this video camera is taking slo-mo shots of my puppy running around, tearing the throat out of his floppy dog, etc. The slow-motion and slow-slow motion modes take more juice, though, so it's good to have an extra charged battery on hand.

I generally take care of my equipment and prefer for it to remain in good order for the entire time I own it, so I always pick up a tablet sleeve even if I rarely bring the device anywhere to begin with. This is a great, basic sleeve - plenty of space, plenty of padding, large zipper for easy zipping, and keeps the tablet out of the sun, dust, and moisture of an indoor environment. Material is a little coarse but doesn't feel cheap. Space for a charging cable and flattish USB charger in the front pocket. The sleeve easily fits my Galaxy Tab S4 while it is in its pseudo-leather case (ASIN: B07GF8K8ZW), which in turn is wide enough to have space for a stylus. .

it is a soft sleeve and not rigid. This means that while you could keep a bare tablet in it, or a tablet with just a thin gel case on it, and it would protect it from the environment and random impacts, I would still recommend getting a proper case for the tablet itself if you are going to be traveling with it.
The only reason this didn't get 5 stars was it requires 2 USB ports to be used for it to function. When someone is already utilizing several USB ports, this can be problematic.

I've owned a few Lexar USB drives and Micro USB drives in the past and they have all had good quality and performance. I've attached the crystal diskmark performance below, but keep in mind that I am using the built-in microsd reader in my computer so speeds may vary as the reader has just as much to do with these benchmarks as the memory card itself.

I don't have any equipment that really stresses the microsd too much. The cameras that I have, while they can record up to 4K at 30fps, have generally had no problem writing to a U1 microsd. The Lexar, which I keep in my Osmo Pocket, is no exception, it has not had an issue recording video.

There is one key thing to point out about Lexar storage media that I've experienced in two of my past devices and that is the built-in expiration or time-bomb (if you don't agree with this philosophy). Lexar seems to have the philosophy that keeping your data intact is the most important when it comes to these products. Solid-state storage media has a theoretical limit to how many times they can be written to. Once that is hit, the media will be permanently damaged. Lexar has written into their firmware, a hard limit that once you write a certain number of times to their media, it will become read-only, keeping your data intact, but the storage unusable from that point on.

While I've experienced failed media in the past, I really only had this behavior with Lexar. I have to say, it did save my wife from losing the pictures on her phone if the card failed instead of becoming read-only.

I have a couple telescopes and several eye pieces/filters that needed one place to stay. Orion makes some great products, but they tend to be fairly pricey when it comes to accessories. This case was half the price of Orion's smallest, so I ordered it. Over all, it seems to work quite nice. It's not the most sturdy of cases, so those who're rough on their equipment might worry some (I'm pretty gentle on my stuff, however. This case comes with a few layers of foam. One of them has pre-cut squares that you can remove for a custom fit. Over all, I found this to be a rather hassle-free, economical solution. It's currently fitting:

*5 1.25" eye pieces (10mm through 25mm,)
*a T-Mount for 35mm cameras,
*a 2x Barlow,
*a light-pollution filter and my polarizing filter (in original cases.

There's room enough for a few more filters (in their original cases) and maybe 3 more larger eye pieces.

I have some Definitive bookshelf speakers. Originally,I got some stands from Best Buy that were very unstable. These are rock solid. There is a fair bit of assembly required and the instructions are C+ quality, but all you need is a philips-head screwdriver. You can finish in < 1 hour.

I have what looks like a standard-height TV stand. I wish these speaker stands were 2"-6" taller.

Works well and have not had any problems with it.  There is a catch though.  The company provides some software for switching between computers with a keyboard sequence.  But, the computer you are switching from must be running and not off or in sleep or hibernate mode. Using the buttons to switch between computers is not the most convenient method.  Apart from that, has been performing as expected, for about a year now.

This camera system builds in the PoE, the one it replaced required a separate switch for that.  The cameras have a clear picture during the day that is definitely 5 stars.  The night vision is 4 stars, but still clear enough to make out faces and license plates, so that's good.  I didn't use the included ethernet cables, but it's nice that it comes with them.  My only complaint is that I can't expand it.  They make 32 camera systems, I wish that the only difference was the number of cameras, because I'd love to expand to 16 or more cameras when I can afford them.  The base systems look the same except for the number of ports, but it does seem like there is a software limitation so I can't move up without replacing the whole system.  One suggestion would be to make the systems able to daisy chain so I could buy a second when I'm ready!  Anyway, that lack of expandibility is the reason I took a star off, if you never will need more than 8 cameras, this is a great choice!

I had a bad experience with my previous Annke security DVR. I could never get it set up with the online viewer, couldn't back it up, and eventually couldn't do a thing with it when the USB port stopped working (you need a mouse). The way I found out the port was no longer working was when I went to review footage of a creep on my porch. Couldn't do it.

So far, this one is lots better. It seems to have a better build quality, and, while set up was not easy, it was doable.

I'm really tired of stuff not working - especially security equipment that, at best, is just okay, and, at worst, does no good whatsoever. If this keeps working, I'll be thrilled.

It does what it says, it connects to a computer via USB, or the USB port on a wall charger, and connects to you phone, tablet, or any other device that requires micro USB for charging.  Works with my fast charger and my Samsung Galaxy S7. Also allows very fast connections from the computer to the phone for file transfer.

I'm a big fan of the 8x32 style of binoculars. These aren't as bright or powerful as the 10x42 or 8x42 binoculars on the market, but they are 1/3 to 1/2 less bulky and lighter weight. I'm more of a hiker than a birder, so when I'm hiking 20 miles, the extra weight and space in my backpack is very noticeable. Realistically, the larger 42mm binoculars are mostly brighter than the 32mm size at dawn and dusk, which is not when I'm hiking. 8x vs 10x is a personal preference, but a lot of people prefer 8x because the image is easier to hand-hold (in addition to the smaller size and lower weight).

Celestron makes a wide variety of binoculars, including a lot of basic-quality entry-level stuff that is not built very well and doesn't perform very well. This TrailSeeker ED model is a big step up from entry-level, both in price and performance. This model isn't quite as good as the top-rated 8x32 models like Nikon Monarch or Zeiss Terra, which both sell for around $400, but I think it is at least as good as any of the competition selling for under $300 that I have tried. I see a bright clear image with no noticeable chromatic aberration. Field of view is much better than most 8x32 binoculars and the image is sharp over a wider area than other under-$300 binoculars that I have tried. Field of view is very useful if your subject moves quickly or unpredictably (birds, wild mammals, sports athletes, etc). Build quality has been very solid and reliable for me so far.

Some people complain that the Celestron warranty is not as good as the competition and this is true. Some of the other brands have a "no questions asked" return policy for a good period time. Celestron's warranty is very limited in comparison, so definitely take that into consideration, especially if you are hard on your equipment.

I received this as a free review sample. As a music stand light it's functional, but not ideal. As a night light or even a clip on to a book for night time reading when your partner of sleeping this is truly useful.

Be aware that it's small and even at max illumination with all LEDs active it is not glaring. That is a good feature, but the tradeoff is as a music stand light you may have to keep adjusting the goosenecks to get optimum illumination.

The goosenecks are a little on the thin side, which is another reason I think this is best suited to clamping directly on a book or headboard (if you can find a spot that the clamp can grip). On a music stand turning pages too briskly can change the position of the LEDs; not a problem when reading a book, but not the distraction you want when playing an instrument.

Bottom line: if you are looking for a light for your music stand carefully comparison shop. If you are looking for a portable and effective reading light you will love this one.

This is a rather nice USB interface VGA webcam with a microscope lens. Once upon a time, instrument makers used the benchtop versions for fine work. From the software included, these were intended for circuit board inspection. They're obsolete now. Someone seems to have bought the leftovers and added a rubbish stand. A decent stand is $21 extra. Since I only spent $18 for the microscope & own plenty of stands, no thanks.

Within those limits, this is a nice little microscope if you have a little patience. You could, for example, use it for showing details on a webchat.
I use these to connect to instruments in my old car, work fine for now.

Even though I have always had an interest in astronomy I was never able to work a course in this subject in my college schedule or afterwards. When I saw this telescope offered I realized that now I had both the time and the means to explore my interest a bit further. I had very little difficulty setting the scope up, and spent some time familiarizing myself with the various components. I practiced using this by checking out objects in my neighborhood, and managed to get an 'up close and personal' view of some birds in a neighbor's yard and quickly realized that this scope was powerful.

That evening I took the scope to an upstairs window to see what I could see, and despite the pesky street light was able to get a great view of the full moon (btw did you know that it sparkles a bit?). I saw details that I had only seen in photos before which was fascinating. Then I decided to take a look at Mars, which was near the Moon that evening. That is when things got complicated. The finder scope and the main scope need to be synced, and I don't know how to do this (yet). With some fiddling, and aided by Mars' close proximity to the Moon I was able to find Mars, which was exciting but for some reason it was distorted (it had a starburst appearance). My husband and I fiddled with various lenses and combinations to try to eliminate this but were unsuccessful. The experimentation was further complicated by the touchiness of the stand....it was difficult to make small, smooth adjustments and to keep the scope locked in position. Some of this is no doubt due to our in expertise, some I think is due to the equipment.

My enjoyment of this scope would have been much greater if more instructions had been provided. We discovered, more or less by accident how to lock, at least partially, the scope into place. We managed to make some focusing adjustments by trial and error. Even some rudimentary instructions in a small booklet or even a sheet or two describing how to adjust, focus and lock the scope as well as an illustration of the scope with all the components clearly labeled with a brief description of their function would have been greatly appreciated. This is a basic instrument, one that will primarily be used by beginners or novices who will not necessarily be familiar with this equipment. Basic instructions should have been included. As it is my unfamiliarity with the various aspects of the telescope make following many of the instructions I do find on-line difficult to follow.

Despite this problems I am enjoying my new toy. I found the stand to be steady, and the tray located on the stand to be a handy place to put lenses and covers. As I mentioned earlier this is a surprisingly (at least to this beginning user) powerful scope. I'm going to play around with this some more, and will probably upgrade some of the lenses and add some accessories based on my experiences. Besides star gazing I think this will be a great item to watch birds or wild life, and it is certainly portable and forgiving enough to take on a camping trip.

This is a nice and sturdy tablet holder that can attach to an instrument stand or any small pipe/bar or even flat surfaces like a desk.  The only issue is that the way the round plastic holder pieces are designed makes it not work so well with some tablets which have rounded corners and very thin bezel like newer samsung ones.  It also doesn't work very well with my surface pro which is too big to fit in the horizontal position.. it can fit vertically but then you lose some rotation capability if you want to rotate it to be horizontal (it only has a 180 degree rotation so you can't flip it all the way around).  It does work well with my smartphone or with smaller tablets like the kindle fire.

Nice wireless keyboard. Easy instant plug and play and good signal connection. Keys press easily but provide nice resistance. Some clicking but isn't overly loud.
Mouse is small and comfortable.
It's a bit annoying that the mouse and keyboard run on a different size of battery (AA and AAA). No off switch either that I found so you have to remove the battery to preserve if you don't use it often.

These headsets are light, comfortable, and do a great job with noise cancellation.

They do NOT have a longer range than my 10 year old Logitechs though, so don't expect the range to be much greater than your basic Bluetooth.

My biggest gripes are:

. When you click on mute in Zoom or Teams with your mouse, you hear a loud MUTED. When you click again, UNMUTED. Every single time. It's super annoying.

. The On and off switch is a tiny slider that you can only really move with your nails, and it has 3 positions, Off, Dongle, Bluetooth. It's easy to pass up the middle position and all together it's not easy and comfortable to turn on and off. And not something you can easily feel for while on your head.

. Finally it doesn't have USB C. In this day and age, why not?

Works great.  multiple USB ports are very useful (was using lap top as charging, and phone, and charging kindle no problem).  One issue is that I was using it to charge my phone at night, and the noise from the converter (i'd say it's louder than lap top fan noise) is a little annoying when you are still in jet lag but trying hard to sleep.

Good value for a keyboard and mouse. The mouse is comfortable to use and quiet. The last mouse I was using had developed a squeak when using the scroll wheel - very annoying. My main complaint about this set is that the keyboard could be much quieter. I work from home and use the keyboard all day long and it does get a little loud sometimes. However, a lot of the quieter keyboards I looked at had a funny keyboard layout. The layout on this keyboard is great and very comfortable to use.

We had a problem that occurred within the first year that required us to return the projector.  BenQ fixed it and sent it back to us.  Other than that one issue, it has been a great purchase. We have owned projectors before, and this one is the cheapest in price and the best in terms of picture that we have ever owned.  We use it all the time. I hope it continues to be a reliable product once we go beyond the 1-year warranty.  It's not too loud, although we live at 4000 feet so I have it in high elevation mode.

Works as advertised. Yes, it is loud. It isn't the lightest in the world. But it works. I use it in a theatre in the booth with all the tech equipment.

The one thing that bothers me is that there is a lock ball on the hose outlet on the main unit. But the pieces that connect have no hole to fit it. So they don't lock on.

Needed to get a case for it. The box it comes in is too small to stuff it all back in each time.

I realize that it is time to let go of the most famous player that is no longer being manufactured, so I wanted to acquaint myself with others and this one is a pretty good start. It does what I need it to do; I connect my headphones and go right to the songs I want to play and they are well organized. The speakers on the device aren't that loud but I never use them anyhow. Storage is good for favorite playlists and this is a very reasonable price.

I so wish they had gone with real wood, this is a beautiful and functional fan.

First and foremost, this is a monopod, and should not be expected to perform the duties of a tripod. The two are not on the same playing field, especially if said field is not level, and the monopod's job is simply to hold the fort when a tripod can't go into battle.

Pros:
1. This monopod comes with its own little stand, and is perfectly capable of standing on its own three feet.
2. It can easily support a DSLR with a medium telephoto lens.
3. Set up is simple, requiring only unscrewing the bottom section, opening the legs and screwing the base back on securely.
4. Extends over six feet tall with two adjustable sections
5. Perfect for concert and theatre events in low or changing light, when a tripod either isn't allowed or is impractical.
6. Great for weddings and museum visits
7. You can sit with the monopod braced against your chair and your feet anchoring the legs for extra stability. (I also use a cable release)
8. Padded grip
9. Handy against attacks by stray animals in the wild.

Cons:
1. At the shortest it's still more than two feet long, and doesn't fit well in the external tripod section of smaller camera bags.
2. It's very heavy for all-day trekking around theme parks, museums, big city tours and the like.
3. No carrying case (but has a strap to fasten it on to stuff)
4. Little legs make a lot of noise when concealed (but see below)
5. A bit tricky on uneven ground if you want to use the legs

Things you can fix:
1. Needs a Quick Release head (albeit adding extra weight and cost)
2. Rattling feet can be muffled with a rubber band

Overall, I'm happy with this monopod, except perhaps for the length and weight. It does a great job when you're rushing around in crowded places where tripods fear to tread.

Amanda Richards, June 19, 2013

The most reliable and solid printer I have ever owned is a Canon Pixma i4500 which sits on my desk and is wired directly to my personal computer. It has been more dependable than any HP or Epson printer I have used and I have used and abused it for years. Because of my experience with my older Pixma, I had very high expectations of the MG5420. For printing, it performs quite well. For scanning, though, it is less than ideal.

Setup of this printer is absurdly easy. I did follow the printed directions, not because I felt like I did not understand the device but because I wanted to determine if the included instructions are useful or if they are somewhat off in their guidance. They took me step by step through configuration, but it could have been summarized as "plug it in, turn it on, follow the instructions on the screen".

This particular printer comes with a black pigment cartridge in addition to 4 color ink tanks. I like this configuration as it means I can print a lot more text pages.

Initial configuration, while straightforward, is lengthy. It takes about 10 minutes of calibration and alignment (during which time it makes all manner of odd noises) before it is ready to go to work. Once it finished configuring itself, I plugged it in to the USB port and Windows 7 loaded drivers from online and it's ready to go. So, if the system has Internet access, the installation media isn't even necessary.

I elected not to set up this printer on wireless, as it will be dedicated to a single machine and as such connected via USB. So, I can't really speak to it's configuration on a wireless LAN.

Print quality is very good. I selected a high-resolution photo and sent it to the printer, and the printer dutifully produced a borderless letter-sized picture with fine detail, even set on regular paper and normal print settings. Color reproduction was slightly dull, though, and I will have to retry with photo paper and photo settings. More astonishing, though, is the print speed - my photo emerged from the printer in roughly 20 seconds, making this one of the fastest color printers I have used for printing photos.

I then decided to scan an image with the printer. The scan was quick and painless. That said, the scan was very banded and the image was marginally acceptable. I tried another scan and got similar results - banding on the image and the overall quality was low. Other reviewers have had good success with the scanning, so I am hopeful that my particular unit is slightly faulty.

I tried using the copy feature using a text-only document and the copy was nearly indistinguishable from the original. Because the copy portion relies on scanning I was unsure if the copy would have the same banding issue - it did not. So, this tells me that in the capacity of a copier this unit is capable of decent OCR work.

My experience with this printer is mostly good. The photo printing and copying is good while the scanning of images leaves something to be desired. Overall, this is a decent printer for moderate use and is worth a look.

I recently upgraded my AV setup and one of the goals was to cut down on the mess of cables connecting everything. While I don't watch tapes very much, I didn't want to eliminate having a VCR since I occasionally will tape shows.

Looked at a variety of VHS/DVD combo units and they all seemed to have their problems. Took a chance on the JVC, and so far (been using it for about 2 months), have been pleased.

The best feature is that it will send both DVD and VHS signals through an HDMI cable. Just one cable connects this to my receiver -- no more tangle of cords! It also will upscale the VHS image but don't expect much. Yes, it's better, but not high def (or even DVD) quality.

The built-in tuner works well for me, but I do live in a fairly strong signal area, so pretty much every tuner works well. The recording feature is pretty easy to use, and the tape-to-DVD dubbing feature is a snap to set up. I've been able to play the disks that I've recorded on other DVD players without any problem.

The remote is not great. Lots of small buttons, and the layout is pretty poor. Load times for DVDs is pretty good. It does make more noise than my other DVD players. Not objectionable, but you can hear the disk spin up. It lags a bit when you hit the eject button. Upscaling for DVDs is decent. Clearly not on a par with an Oppo, but a solid performer.

While there are better choices out there for just a DVD player, just a DVD recorder, or just a VHS player, this is a good choice if you're looking for a single player that does all the above, plus offers a built-in tuner and single-cable connectivity.

Lastly, this is also sold at Sam's Club. You may want to check them out for pricing. Amazon also offers a pretty good price as well.

UPDATE: There's a firmware update available that fixes the problem with the recording shutting down in mid-program. According to JVC, it seems that some commercials trigger the copy-protection system, and it stops recording. It happens very infrequently, but the firmware update solves the problem. Easy to install -- just download the file from the JVC site, burn it to a CD, and pop it in. Full instructions come with the firmware file. Not essential to do unless you're having the problem of shutdowns mid-program.

Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

So far so good!

I recently purchased a new zoom lens for my camera after I broke the old one when I took a tumble. I had filters like these for my old lens but the thread size was different so my old filters were no longer useful. I selected this filter for my new lens, somewhat apprehensively because of the relatively low asking price. It has proven to be a decent filter but it is not useful in all situations.

The idea behind this filter is light diffusion which will give an image a very slight haze or softness, depending on the lighting and subject. This is an effect that can be emulated in software during post-processing but in doing this type of enhancement I have found it is sometimes unnatural. It certainly is less fun than making it happen while shooting, which is why these types of filters are available.

In use it works, though I have had mixed results. When using it with certain light sources, the filter seems to have no real effect at all, while with others it creates a subtle, soft glow around the subject. I am still working out the situations where it is most effective. I have had similar issues with filters like these with other lenses, and as such I assume the problem is in my lack of practice with them. It will take some time and practice to make my results more consistent, and for now I lay the fault on myself.

The build quality seems to be good. I have received filters in the past where the glass rattles in the frame which is unsettling. This one is tight and there is no play between the glass and the frame. It screws on to the lens securely and is easy to clean.

The asking price is quite reasonable. I have seen these filters priced much higher, and I have also seen much cheaper ones that do not work well. The pricing seems in line with the product, if not slightly low.

I have no complaints with this filter. The issues I have with it are probably my inexperience, and I will keep working with it to improve my results. I will return here and update my review if my impression changes. For now, though, I am satisfied.

My family got together and picked this up for me during Fuji's sale/promotion in March. This is going to cover Christmas and birthdays for the next few years :)

I've found that backing off the connection a 1/4 inch or so keeps the hood from rattling and still keeps it firmly in place.
