Highly recommended.

Overall this is a nice affordable zoom lens.  The aperture is nice and big offering great light collection. Used with my Celestron astromaster 130EQ, it doesn't maintain focus across the entire zoom range, requiring about a quarter turn of focus adjustment from 8 mm to 24 mm.  And yes mine does rattle too.  There are four lenses total, and the spacers and mechanisms aren't well-matched.  But none of this really impacts the quality of the images.  I unscrewed it all and tightened it which helped some, but not much.  I use some basic eyeglass lens cleaning wipes which unfortunately introduced more lint than it removed.  The Eclipse cleaning solution works well combined with a lint-free pad.  The focal points across the range typically focus precisely on at least one of the lens surfaces.  Which means that any tiniest piece of lint or speck can foul an image, especially bright ones.  So be prepared for that, and if the internal lenses are clean and you're trying to fix a slight rattle by opening it up, my advice is don't!  This aside, the lenses themselves are good quality, and I'm pleased with the bright sharp images and large field of view I can get with this zoom lens for the price.

When purchasing a bluetooth mouse, or any bluetooth device, an important factor is how well it connects and how well it STAYS connected. After all this time, the industry still can’t make up its mind about how bluetooth works:
- Microsoft with their mouse and Sony with their controller that pair without the need of a code (which Android’s bluetooth stack doesn’t support).
- Mice and keyboards that will not reconnect after it wakes from sleep mode.
- To this day, bluetooth devices still can’t wake a computer from suspend state.
So when I get a simple bluetooth mouse for a good price, and it actually works as expected, I was happy.

For my review, I’m comparing the Bornd mouse to the [[ASIN:B006428K7I Motorola 89519N Bluetooth Mouse]] which I got in a set that included the [[ASIN:B004L9MBH6 Motorola Wireless Keyboard for Motorola ATRIX and XOOM (Motorola Retail Packaging)]].

With the Motorola mouse, its frequency somehow conflicts with the Motorola keyboard, resulting in sticky keys, as in “I’m having a good daaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaay”. Conversely, the keyboard interferes with the mouse where the computer would actually lose connection with the mouse for a few seconds after typing, or lose connection completely.

What I liked about the Bornd:
- Pairing was simple using the button at the bottom of the mouse.
- Operating distance is about 5 feet, but this may be because of my computer’s bluetooth antenna
- Takes a single AA battery which lasts over a month of moderate use (2 hours per day)
- Mouse movement is good. No need to adjust mouse speed in the control panel.
- Accuracy is good. Editing images using Pixlr.com, I’m able to select precisely the parts of the image I need.

What gave me trouble with the Bornd:
- When you first put your hand on this mouse, you will not feel that it is very well built. The plastic is completely smooth and the mouse wheel seems to rattle when you shake it. I got used to it after a few minutes, though.
- The mouse reconnects with the computer most of the time, but sometimes it was necessary to turn the mouse off and on again after the computer reboots or if the computer was out of range for an extended period of time.
- Lately, I’ve been experiencing double-clicks when I click on the left mouse button once. I’m usually able to fix this by getting angry and slamming the mouse down a couple of times. This may indicate a build quality issue with this mouse.

In my specific case, the Bournd did not interfere with my Motorola keyboard at all and it seems the sticky key occurs only when the batteries on the keyboard runs low.

Summary:
I bought this kit because I needed to recover the data on an 80GB Hitachi 1.8" Drive from a dead Vaio notebook. No setup was required after I finished installing the drive in the enclosure, and it was recognized and read on my XP machine without a fuss. The enclosure is a thin aluminum extrusion with channels on the inside. The end caps appear to be pot metal castings. One end cap contains the interface board with LED activity light and the USB connector. A USB cable is provided. The kit is cheaply made but did what I needed.

Installation:
Installation consisted of mating a flex cable and connector, sliding the drive and active end cap into the enclosure, and screwing in the end cap(s).

It takes a bit of care and patience to insert the flex cable into the connector on the drive, but I was able to get it done in a few minutes.
The cable needs to be made to assume an S-bend after attaching it to the drive so that the entire assembly will fit into the box. That is best accomplished by gently pushing the end cap and HDD together and guiding the cable into an S. I suggest you place the assembly next to the enclosure first so you can see how much length the bend will need to take up. It's not much. Then, slide the drive into the enclosure followed by the cable and end cap, gently guiding the cable bend as needed. Make sure the end cap fits properly in place before and while you install the screws.

Here's the part I deducted a star for: The screws go into unthreaded channels in the enclosure and their alignment is less than perfect. It took quite a while and a better screwdriver than is provided to get the screws fully seated. YMMV.

If the drive rattles around more than you like front to back, you may wish to install one or two of the stick-on rubber bumpers that are provided onto the far end of the HDD or the inside of the blank end cap. Be aware you'll have to deal with two more screws if you put them inside the end cap.

I'm a smaller woman, and found the grip on my Canon 30D to be uncomfortable, but I wasn't willing to compromise on photo quality so a digicam was out. When I discovered micro four thirds cameras, I tried out the Oly E-P1 and E-LP1, but preferred the feel of the GF1. I also tried out the Samsung NX10, but it just doesn't offer enough native lenses for me.

The GF1 is the most comfortable camera I've ever owned. The image quality is very good, and although I hear it's good on full auto, I use mine on full manual or shutter priority, and it's very easy to use if you've had any experience with a full featured camera. The buttons and menus are very intuitive, the wheel at the top of the camera is easy to use and I like the flash to use as a fill flash. At default I got a few blown highlights, but this is very easy to control by stepping down just a little.

The only things that I didn't love are the rear dial - it's a little more recessed than I'd like, although I got used to it pretty quickly - and I would have preferred a flip and twist screen since the camera doesn't come with a view finder. Otherwise I'm very satisfied with this camera.

The 14-45mm kit lens is good quality. It's solid with no rattles, turns with just enough resistance, and takes sharp high quality pics with very little chromatic aberration.

One thing last worth mentioning is the stabilization. It's in the lens, and it works better than I expected. I got handheld pics reliably at speeds I haven't been able to shoot at before. That being said, if you prefer your stabilization in the camera rather than in the lens, the E-PL1 is definitely worth checking out.

I'm very happy with the GF1, particularly the easy menus and controls. It takes the annoyances out of photography so I can concentrate on taking the pics rather than fighting the camera. With good image quality, nice videos, fast auto focus and better than average auto features, this seems like a camera for anyone interested photography, from newbie to pros looking for a smaller second camera. For enthusiasts like me, it's just the ticket!

I bought this SDR device so I could listen to shortwave radio but I still can't get that band to work. I have tried the HDSDR software and some other software but it only seems to go as low as 25MHZ. I tried switching where the antenna is connected and it doesn't make a difference. It works a lot better than my other SDR device and has better reception but neither of my SDR devices will pick up shortwave. Is there a software or setting that you recommend for this??

One other issue I noticed is the board inside the case seems loose. It rattles around. This isn't a big problem, just something I want to note. It has had a software crash a couple of times and I'm wondering if the loose board is causing this...

So far I am really liking this SDR device though...

Sennheiser has a wonderful range of headphones from studio-quality to sports, and these headphones have the same lush sound sound as a pair of their high-end cans but pared down to earbud size and for those on the go who don't want to skimp on quality.

The calls and pairing was simple, clear and crisp and nice bass as well. I like to wear these on my morning and afternoon runs and the price for these is excellent.

I was looking for a simple sort of cd clock radio to keep on a nightstand.  It's amazing how difficult it was to find something like that that fit my needs, and I ended up with this unit although I really wasn't intrested in the iPhone/iPod connections.  I went to a local electronics store and first tried a litte Sony machine, was set to buy it, and then the salesman showed me this Phillips unit.  The sound was overwhelmingly better on the Phillips unit.  I admit I'm not an audiophile, but I just want something that sounds good when I played CDs at bedtime.  I quickly dismissed the little Sony and went for this unit.  Since having it about a week now, I really like the sound from the CD player.  I did try my iPhone 4 on it to see if it would connect, and it did and it played music like a champ.  Strong and clear.  I have a rubber bumper on my iPhone and had to remove it to make the phone fit properly but that's no big deal.  In fact what I'm thinking of doing is reprogramming my older iPhone (first generation) with nothing but music on it and leaving that plugged in the Phillips unit.  I keep my iPhone 4 in a different charger in a different room so it doesn't disrupt my sleep AND so I won't forget it when I'm leaving the house.  So far I'm a happy camper with this little Philips unit.  The only con is the brightness of the backlit display which is rather bright.  I placed the unit in a different part of the room where the remote still works but the brightness of the display doesn't affect my sleep.  I like a dark room!

I bought this particular receiver for my 85 year old mother. Her old "Scott" receiver finally bit the dust. She has a lot of vinyl records and I needed a receiver which I could connect a turn-table too and this one has phono outputs.

I had it shipped to her house and after I arrived I had it set up in about 15 minutes. I didn't even have to read the directions as it was pretty straightforward. I also connected a CD player and the receiver has plenty of outputs. It's kind of heavy but that wasn't a problem. After it was all connected I turned it on and *voila!* music! She's hard of hearing so I had to crank it up and it sounded great! I can't remember the size of the two speakers but they are probably around 25 years old, big (sit on the floor) and this receiver powered them just fine.

Mom can't quite understand how to work the radio....that could have been designed a lot more simply but I set it to her favorite station and she was fine. I did have to consult the directions to figure out how to use and preset radio stations. It was not intuitive at all.

Overall, it's a nice receiver. It's not what a true audiophile would buy, but it was a great replacement for a very old receiver.

This little stereo is adequate. I can play radio, my cd's or a cassette. The sound quality is best on commercial cd's. There is no adjustment of the sound except volume. I wish there was a mixer but for the price it's a good little workhorse.

What I like about this watch:
- one full charge lasts several days
- good way to track your BPM, Blood pressure, calories burn, steps taken
- could make phone calls with the watch
- if you take the watch off for whatever reason (like to shower) it doesn't keep taking your BMP or blood pressure so you don't have to worry about your data getting messed up/ inaccurate.
- comfortable silicone band which has a lot of holes to adjust to your size wrist, I have a very small wrist and use the second to last hole
- good size screen, not too large and not too small
- you could set alarms (through the app) also features a stop watch and timer
- receive and check notifications for several apps plus text messages
- has a find phone feature if you misplace your phone
- you could add music to your phone (which I have not done, and not sure if I'm going to do)
- waterproof
- Compatible with my Samsung smartphone, and easy to set up
- Great to have at work, to keep track of time and if I receive any messages/notifications on my phone without having to check my phone

dislike:
- only 4 different dial face designs to choose from
- speaker is towards the bottom so sound could be blocked by your arm depending on your position
- sleep tracker is not very accurate (while I'm laying in bed reading, watching a movie, or on my phone it thinks I am sleeping, and there is no way to edit the hours manually)
- no power button (to turn on or off)
- you cannot name or write notes with the alarms, there are only icons to label
- does not stay connected to my phone in my whole house. If I have my phone on charge in my living room and I'm in my kitchen which is 2 rooms over, I will not get notifications from my phone
- app doesn't not always update, I will have to go to the app and refresh (down swipe) for data to refresh and update
- charger connection is magnetic and a couple times it was bumped while on charge and the charger got knocked off and I didn't know, do it wasnt charging. Plus if the charger breaks for whatever reason I don't have a back up.

I’m not a sound snob, so I can’t speak to the sound quality of these headphones. To me, they sound just fine. I use them almost every night, either paired with my laptop or phone.

The active noise cancelling feature is my favorite. I’ve tried similar features on other headphones and sometimes I get nauseated after having the noise cancelling on for too long. I don’t have that problem with these headphones. The active noise cancelling doesn’t block out all sound, but it does a decent job.

The ear cups are round and nicely padded. The headphones aren’t too tight on my head, either. If you have a larger head, this pair of headphones might not be too comfortable, as the ear cups are on the small side.
I brought this speaker for My Wallmount TV. This speaker perfectly to my LG TV and sound quantity is pretty clear. I can play music from my iPhone and iPad as well.

Sounds quality is good and I like that I can comfortably fit my sunglasses under the headset.  My only complaint is it's a little too big for my head! I don't think I have an abnormally small head (5'3 female) so i'm surprised that I can't adjust it to a shorter length. That can be annoying sometimes as it will start to slide down.
I only paid $11 when I got it and the current price tag seems a bit crazy high.  The Sony cable is durable and delivers decent/crystal sound quality.

This should go without saying, but you need a smart phone or smart device to use these cameras.

Creating an account is free, each camera comes with a free 30 day trial of the premium service, after that the premium service is a charge per camera. This model, the Kasa Spot, does not have a free subscription available.

The app does a great job of walking you through set up of each camera. There are sticker templates so you space the included screws properly to mount the cameras, which the app also walks you through. I found that to be really helpful since I’ve never installed anything like these cameras before. One of the cameras had problems setting up, but the app still walked me through resetting and trying again. Even for an inexperienced person such as myself, the set up was extremely easy with no need to contact technical support. For a tech savvy person, the install would be a breeze.

You can set privacy settings, so certain cameras only record sound or video, and you can set “activity zones” for cameras to focus on, excluding the rest of the field of vision.

This model is an “indoor” camera. It’s not weatherproof, but if you have front windows (like I do), you can install an indoor camera to view outdoor areas.

I like the look but actually causes some issues. The slick polished aluminum frame is hard to handle, I drop it on my desk because it slipped out of my hand. There is no power switch like I have on all my WD drives.  I wouldn’t get this to mobile with but for you desk or a static location should be fine and would look really nice. Data transfer speeds meet today’s standards, I was able to transfer about 1.5 TBs of photos and video in about 4 hours, at speeds about 143 MB/s. If you want to put this on your desk I can see where the look would be a selling point, if this will be tucked away somewhere than there may be more affordable options at 4 TBs.

I'd been using the same router that the cable company installed when I signed my contract back in 2009. I figured that any 2016 entry level router should be a noticeable upgrade. I've had movies stall in the middle of streaming, etc.

This was a quick and easy install and yes, i'm not getting as much movie stalling...but it still happens occasionally. So I'm satisfied, but not ecstatic. I was hoping to eliminate stalling completely. Still, it does seem to be better. Maybe I should have tossed in the next $50 for the better version...I'll keep that in mind for when 2022 rolls around and it's time to upgrade again.

Unit looks really cool.

Instructions for this item were really clear and it was easy to setup. All I had to do was remove the plastic strips from the under the ear buds then they pair with the case. Then I turned my bluetooth on and found the item and they paired to my phone without any problem (I have a Samsung Galaxy S10+). I would have given 5 stars but the tap functions dont work so well. You are supposed to tap twice to pause or play music. This usually worked about 3 out of 5 when I tested on both ear buds. I tapped faster and slower to see if that would change the results, but it didnt. When it came to the three taps for previous/next song, the ear buds seemed confused and began pausing and playing the music at times. Again, I couldn't tell if I was tapping too fast or slow. This functions worked about 1-2 times out of 5 tries. The range is great though. I was able to leave my phone on my bed and walk out my front door (about 20 ft away) then outside to my front door and there was no static or insidication that the connection was fading. The volume is great as well with both or one ear bud in.

Recently my husband purchased a touch screen computer for my art studio for the whopping sum of 60.00 USD! I was ecstatic till I realized that there are only 4 usb ports to the sweet little machine and I am a peripherals l junkie. What is a girl to do? I purchased this Hub (and one other brand).. Good product but at highway speeds it is difficult to hear. Possible issue with install but every now and then I can hear static. Overall great unit and very user friendly. Great battery life. Just needs to be a little louder.

I installed this system on my 2007 Ford Ranger.  Pretty simple install, pulled the tail light, found the backup lamp hot line, tapped in, reinstalled the tail light, mounted the camera above the license plate, plugged in the monitor, but the truck in reverse, magic, there it was!  The picture get a bit noisy (static) depending on the parking location and the amount of metal around, but it shows adequately enough to back up and park.  I do wish the parking lines were more adjustable, but I get that it can't be perfect for every vehicle.  This does well enough for my needs and the price was right.

This is really quite large. I mean, that's a good thing if you have a lot of AC adapters that all manage not to block each other on here (and some still will), but it's not great when depth is tight behind your stereo or wherever you're trying to hide this. The flat plug is much appreciated, as is being white. The USB ports are becoming still more useful, but I wouldn't get them unless you plan to use them (like, if you're using this in a static setup with no need for ports, why waste even a tiny bit of power - and space). And the switch is good for some scenarios and terrible for others, so contemplate that as well before you jump into anything.

It's very lightweight. I guess it doesn't need to be heavy.

I lived and breathed full-sized Kensington trackball mice from about 1987 until my last one stopped functioning and I couldn't find them anymore...probably in the late '90s. Tried some others; all had small, lightweight balls that gave none of the feel and control of Kensinton's...Expert Mouse? Was that what it was called back then too? Because it was the same general design as the current Expert Mouse, but the body was computer-case white.

Anyway, I had several of those (the quality going downhill with each iteration, as I recall) and loved them, and since they disappeared (as far as I could tell), I adapted, first to trackpads, which I've never liked much, and then back to traditional mice which don't give nearly the control of a trackball. Now, at last, it seems Kensington has again begun to produce truly worthwhile trackball mice, and this is one. Oh, it's _so_ good to have one of these again.

I'm doing that thing I hate when other people do it and reviewing the product as soon as I've gotten it up and running, without any kind of experiential history behind my assessment. I'll come back and update this in the future if necessary. But so far: I'm happy, happy, happy to have a real, full-sized Kensington trackball mouse again, with a heavy, substantial ball. There are only two things about this device that I'm not crazy about: In my old Kensington mice, the ball rested on physical rollers and I could give the ball a good spin and it would keep spinning for a second before stopping; it spun much more freely in its cavity than this ball does (so far...maybe that's something that will break in?) [Update: yes, after about three days of use the ball rolls more smoothly and silently than the old one on rollers ever did]. And the other thing is the scrolling mechanism. It's weird. Despite the KensingtonWorks software trying to make us believe otherwise, the "scroll ring" itself actually has nothing to do with scrolling, nor with anything else - the "scroll ring" is not even a control, but just a static piece of chrome trim. What makes the mouse scroll is twisting the ball this way or that from the top, as if it were a knob. At first I thought the "scroll ring" wasn't working because I was trying to use it without touching the ball...which does nothing. And now that I've figured out how scrolling works (you rest your finger on the "scroll ring" and push and pull the side of the ball)...I'm not crazy about it. I'm getting used to it, but it's just a weird way to scroll (I can't for the life of me remember how I used to do it on the Expert Mouse decades ago). It does work though.

(Update on the scrolling: I'm also not crazy about the way the KensingtonWorks software handles the scrolling speed adjustment. When you make the base pointer movement speed faster, the pointer continues to move smoothly, but just faster. When you make the scrolling speed faster though, you lose all smoothness - the software makes the scrolling faster by breaking it into successively larger and more jarring jumps. At the slowest speed, it's pretty smooth; at the highest speeds it's no longer really scrolling, but simply jumping abruptly from one screenful (or page) to the next. Increasing the scrolling speed just increases the size of these jumps, but I find them jarring and annoying starting at the second or third lowest speed setting.)

I also had to figure out how to program one of the buttons as a click lock, since Kensington doesn't call it that anymore, but calls it "left drag", "right drag", and "middle drag" (and I have no idea what the difference is between those three - I just chose "left drag" and it's working fine).

So far, those are my only gripes, all minor. So happy to have one of these things again! =) (Did I mention that?)

Enjoy...

Great set of Bluetooth earbuds.  When I am talking through the earbuds, my volume is normally on low. Even with a low setting, the people I am having a conversation can hear people across the street on the basketball courts.  It does pick up your surroundings well.  No static.  Very clear voice.  It is waterproof  I did shower with them on.  Only issue was that it turns off when the water hits it.  Unsure if it’s because it’s water or because it thinks I pushed them to turn it off. That’s why I am giving it a four star.

I was definitely surprised how inexpensive and still pretty good this dual monitor mount is.  Admittedly, it is not as slick as the ones that cost 4-6 times the price, but it is still relatively acceptable in most situations.  As another reviewer mentioned, I'm not certain it will hold the weight of some 27" monitors well.  I've seen better cable organization, although this one's is not bad, and it does not seem as smoothly and infinitely adjustable as one of the high end models.  All that said, if you just have two mid-size monitors you want to mount in very static positions, this is a great way to clear up some desk space.

I wanted to listen to old cassette tapes but I have no stereo system available and I didn't want to buy one just for this purpose. This old players are still useful for basic listening and recording. The front speaker is a little tinny but I didn't expect more. The price was right, too.

My 8-year-old loves books on CD, so we got this to replace our old player. It's perfect. Kiddo has been carrying it around and keeps swinging it by the wrist strap but the player doesn't skip a beat! The controls are easy to use. There is some processing time between functions, the computer is not very fast. It feels very durable.

The speaker is mediocre, but you can hear the words just fine; it's tinny as expected for something like this. It is what it is. Plugging in headphones works great.

The one issue we have is that the Bluetooth doesn't seem to be able to pair with objects that can't "pick" it. Because my headphones just pair with whatever picks it, the two devices just have the Bluetooth lights blink until they time out. The manual only says to pick it in the menu, but all my Bluetooth devices are old and just have a pairing function, no menus. There is not much information for troubleshooting so we gave up. I docked one star for that.

I received this item for free through Vine for an unbiased review, my opinion is my own.

What sets the INNOCN 15.6" portable monitor apart from other type-c portable monitors is the built in battery and the touch screen features. In the box, a soft silicone case is included with a cover that folds into a stand, making it feel like an oversized tablet.

Other portable monitors with built-in battery are usually a little bit thicker or have a bulge at back of the screen. The INNOCN doesn't have that. It is a thin slab that is around 3/8" thick. I actually use it as a secondary screen on a daily basis and while the monitor has an all aluminum casing, there is almost no heat generated by the screen during use.

The touch capability of this monitor brings touch support to any Windows PC without the need for drivers but even more, connect this to an Android phone such as my LG V40 and not only does the phone go into desktop mode, the touch screen works to turn the phone into a 15.6" tablet! The built-in battery will help to keep the phone topped off and allow fully wireless (no need to plug into the wall, but there will be a wire between phone and screen) tablet.

My previous monitor was a LePow 15.6" type-c portable Monitor. It is representative of many other portable monitors on the market. Compared to the INNOCN, the INNOCN is a lot brighter and the colors more vibrant. The LePow was instant on but the INNOCN can take about 2-3 seconds to turn on after receiving a signal. Both have speakers that are tinny and quite weak, but serviceable if you're on-the-go.

If you are purchasing this monitor to work with the Nintendo Switch, you will be disappointed. The Switch is very picky about the conditions that must be met before it goes into docked mode, mainly a 19v type-c PD. The power output from this monitor simply doesn't supply that, even when plugged in to an original Nintendo power adapter (the adapter will serve to charge the screen, but will not supply the 19v to the connected switch). It will only work with the switch through a dock, which really defeats the purpose of a portable monitor. On the other hand, the LePow does actually does work with the switch. Connected a power adapter or portable phone charger to the LePow and the monitor will supply the necessary 19v to the Switch.

So overall, a great monitor for most uses, especially the ability to turn a phone into a large touchscreen tablet, but if you want a portable large-screen solution for the Nintendo Switch, go for something like the LePow

The BOIFUN Portable Monitor really IS portable. It’s not that much bigger than my 13-inch MacBook Pro, and it weighs less. I could see packing the monitor for a trip, to use for work and play. I have used the monitor with my Mac and my Nintendo Switch, and it works great with both devices.

The monitor has USB-C and Mini HDMI input options. It comes with cables for both options, which I appreciated. That’s one small downside, you’ll need to make sure to take the Mini HDMI cable with you.

I used the USB-C input with my Mac, it worked. I used the Mini HDMI to HDMI input for my Nintendo Switch, it worked. With both devices, the picture on the monitor was clear and bright. The monitor is plug and play, no instructions really needed.

I did some online Splatoon matches with my Switch to see if there would be any noticeable lag or freezing on the monitor, there were no problems. The game looked great, although the built-in speakers are very tinny.

I do have a few complaints about the monitor. The “smart cover” is super basic. The pictures show folding the cover and using it as a stand, propping the monitor against it. Like a tablet smart cover. But that’s seemingly impossible to do. The cover is very floppy, with no support to hold itself in any stand-shape. The box does include a basic plastic stand, but I wish I could use the cover as pictured, since the stand is one more thing to pack if I go somewhere.

Also, the cover is like a file folder. There’s no way to attach it to the monitor. It relies on magnets alone to stay in place. I wish it had some sort of clip or strap inside, to secure the monitor.

Secondly, the input ports are on opposite sides. The USB-C port is on the same side as the power port, but the Mini HDMI port is on the other side. So if you want to use the monitor in landscape position, you’re limited by input type.

The monitor is powered via USB-C, a cable and wall adapter are included. The wall adapter is a basic 5V USB-A wall adapter. I like that it isn’t some proprietary charging cable.

Works well with all Apple devices, Great treble. Takes less than 1 minute to sink with any Apple device. The stand is metal and durable and  comes with a speaker application with said Apple devices so you can talk in phone conversations---very clear!!!

When it comes to movies, these speakers are amazing. Like being in a theatre all by yourself. You can hear every word clearly through the centre speaker, and the subwoofer can shake the house if you're not careful.
However, it is less than amazing for music, as it is deficient in the tweeter category, so your treble gets lost.
Movie buffs and gamers can rejoice - music fans won't be ecstatically happy.

Nice, robust case. Used it on a Samsung Tab A. It fit perfectly. People absolutely need to watch the video showing how to install the tablet. It is an easy install when you follow the directions. The video also nicely illustrates the right way and the wrong way to use the built in tablet stand that is part of the Seymac cover. I had one problem with the volume buttons not aligning properly with the tablet. The Seymac customer service people are sending me a new cover but in the meantime i cut two small pieces of a wine cork (no shortage of them in our house) and used them to make the alignment work at least for the time being. All you need is a knife, a cutting board and a cork. I would buy thus cover again.

Earlier this year I purchased this (880) at a truck stop. I use the radio occasionally, mainly for work communication between transport and chase vehicles.
It so far it has been a very good purchase. Its held up well to construction work (heavy equipment movement). I have had no issues with the radio at all.

I think the stock speaker has too low of a volume (well for fast approaching 50 it is). I purchased a remote speaker and mounted it in the rear window area of my truck (F150) I have no trouble hearing now, as I often have to turn it down. The remote speaker works well when you have the car radio lightly playing on the long trips. Then the iPhone giving NAV reports over the car stereo speakers too (CarPlay). That remote speaker still allows plenty of volume to properly hear your other vehicle.

Since my job varies and I don't always need this unit hooked up, or for quick changes. I elected for a slightly different approach. I used 3 magnetic car phone mounts and attached them to the front slide out cup holder assembly of the F150. The magnets will latch onto the radio allowing me to choose various angles of mounting it at. We always run ch 19 so really changing or seeing the display while driving is almost always not necessary for me. However it is easily accessible if needed. I find it helps cut down on the amount of light distractions with the unit side ways. Though the CB does have day/night mode if you want to use it.

I have not seen any issues with the CB and the magnetic mounts. The 3 mounts have held the radio in some bumpy construction, terrain and it hasn't fallen off yet.

I am not by any means a power user, I just need a good, well made, radio that will hold up over time. This unit fits the bill.
I misplaced my original headphone cable which had a volume control switch attached to it. This model doesn't have a volume control switch.

There is a lot to like with this computer: The small size is great. There are 2 USB-C ports instead of just 1 like with a lot of others. There is no bloatware. You can hook up your monitor to either the DisplayPort or USB-C connection. They include a USB-C to HDMI adapter. There are 4 USB 3.0 ports. Good speed for regular computer use with the I7 processor and SSD.

The biggest thing to dislike is the volume of the fan. You wouldn't think a computer this small would have such a loud fan, but it does. It's annoyingly loud. If you're going to be working on the computer a lot while in a silent room, I would recommend to not buy this computer because of the fan noise.

The Logitech Folio Touch is a JOY to type on. I really love typing on it — I’m writing this review using the case. I’ve typed quite a few long documents on it. I turn to this keyboard when I want distraction-free writing.

The keyboard reminds me of Apple laptop keyboards before the disastrous butterfly keyboards. The keyboard is backlit, and the brightness of the backlighting can be adjusted via the function keys. The row of function keys is another good feature for me. I find it much faster and easier to adjust the iPad’s brightness or volume using the function keys.

I downloaded the Logitech Control app, but it doesn’t seem to give any options for customizing the keyboard. All I see the app do is check for keyboard firmware updates. When I wanted to change the trackpad scrolling direction, I had to hunt through the iPad’s settings — I thought that would be in the Logitech app. (I learned those settings became part of iOS, so the Logitech app seems … unnecessary.)

I don’t really like the trackpad. I’ve used Logitech mice for years. My current daily mouse is the Logitech MX Master 3, so I *know* they can do a good Mac mouse. But I just feel like they dropped the ball with this trackpad. The trackpad works but it could be better. I notice drag at times, and I don’t like the noise or tactile feedback when I click it. I can adjust a few settings (scrolling direction, tracking speed, tap to click, and two finger secondary click) in the iPad’s General Settings, but I want to be able to customize more through Logitech.

The corners of the case are reinforced. The bumper is a bit thick, too thick for some hubs or USB-C cables to fit without using an extension cable. There is a cutout for the power button so Touch ID can be used. There’s a spot for the Apple Pencil, it can rest inside the bumper or fit through a slot on the latch.

The Folio Touch pairs via the Smart Connector, so it’s super easy to set up: just stick your iPad inside and it’s ready to go. The iPad powers the keyboard, so I don’t have to remember to charge it, which I like. I haven’t noticed it being a battery hog.

Overall, I really like the Logitech Folio Touch. I actually use my iPad more now, since I like typing on the keyboard so much. The case has made my iPad more functional for me.
Works well but the volume seems a bit low. Getting it into the mic holder is very difficult and once in you'll not want to take it off.
Easy to use. Volume control is low and can't be overridden so on the plane it was hard to hear.  Quality was good. Holds up in luggage and with a 3 yr old.
Volume diminished after 2 months
Worked really well the entire length of a 15 hour car trip and back. The volume may come back a little low when traveling at highway speeds, or maybe my car is just noisy.

First the pros:

Inexpensive (mine was $23)
Excellent radio
Good video quality (Not iPhone quality, but certainly not too much less)
Large memory
Mostly intuitive controls (although it has some odd symbols)
Light

Now the cons:

The headphone jack is located on the bottom of the unit. This makes it odd to change, say, volume while it is in your pocket.
There is no cover for the mini USB port, so that could get dirty.

Recap:
Just as I bought this, I was given a new iPod Shuffle which goes for about twice the price. The Shuffle beats this unit as far as quality and ease of use goes, but cannot compare to this unit's features. Apple obviously spent a lot of time making a good product a great product while Coby spent a lot of time cutting corners on the little things to stuff more features in, turning a potentially great product into a good product. Still, if you want lots of features and don't want to cough up the money for an iPod Classic, this could be the product for you. Just as a note though, iPod Shuffle earbuds don't work so great with this thing, although other earbuds do.

I have been building computer systems and troubleshooting for a long time. I really enjoy taking parts in and out and programming systems to do what I want. I remember looking at a commercial for the new tablets and saying to my family- "What the heck would anyone want one of THOSE things for?" It was not long after they became bored with my insistence that tablets were a total waste that I had my chance to take my first tablet for a test run- the Acer Iconia A1-830.

The Acer was a fantastic little first tablet. It performed as well or better than a few Samsungs and older Apples that we had the chance to put it up against, and for the price, it was a great little tablet. I found some use for it and found myself reaching for the tablet when I didn't want to do work at the computer. It was more portable than a laptop and easier to do quick surfing and simple tasks on, and GAMING.

I thought that all was well until I began to have a few issues with the Acer. It was at that point that I saw a great price on the new Samsung Galaxy Tab S2. I was hooked.

WHAT IS THIS TABLET LIKE?
I plan to write this review to people who are not as interested in the detailed specs of this unit, but instead I will write this for an average user who might not be as technically astute. There are quite a few well done reviews that have lots of specs and details that will satisfy those who really need that information to make decisions.

SCREEN
One of the things that I did not like about the older Samsungs was the size. I preferred the more squared screen of the Acer than the Samsungs I had worked on. My daughter has one and although it seems nice, I just was not keen on the screen. This model has exactly what I wanted to have. The shape makes it easier to work on the web , use as an E reader, and play games. I find it easier to read than more elongated screens.

One of the things that I found to be frustrating is the slick surface of the screen. For web surfing or book reading it is fine, but games can really get frustrating as I find the screen to be very sensitive and it is easy to mess up.

As for the brightness, it is very bright. I have it turned down by about 75% and it is plenty bright enough most of the time. Also, the color contrast is breathtaking. The screen is very sharp and the blacks are BLACK and the colors are very saturated. This thing is eye candy squared! It is hard to look at other screens when I am done using this.

COLOR
This is not really gold in color. I would say it is gold tinged platinum in color. Do not expect a bold gold.

SMOOTHNESS AND UNEVEN EDGES
There are a few things which bug me about this tablet, but not that much. Getting a good case from Fintie took care of it. The button on the bottom of the vertical positioned screen stands out from the unit. That means if you are going to get a keyboard in the case, it could press on the button and cause problems. The Fintie case is raised enough to protect the button.

There is also the camera lens on the back that sticks out quite a bit. Again, the case takes care of that problem. The back itself might be plastic, but it feels like metal and looks like metal so it is not cheap looking.

SPEED AND FUNCTION
WOW is this thing FAST! I have to say that it really has blown me out of the water with the speed and smooth operation of everything I have tried to do. It works smoothly, load up is fast. I know part of that might be due to the inclusion of Lollipop but also the hardware and set up. I have not found it to lag at all. Great performance. I also know that this model is scheduled for the Marshmallow upgrade sometime this year which could change performance to be even better.

I have 32G microSD card in this right now but it is expandable to 128.

BATTERY LIFE
I was very concerned about all of the complaints about battery life. I was so concerned I almost didn't get this tablet. I am SO glad I did, however. I keep location turned off and bluetooth as well unless I am using it. The battery stuns me with how long it has lasted. I loaded that baby up to 100% last night and this morning about 11 AM I began to work intensely on the tablet, trying to back up files from my Acer and transfer them over to the Samsung via bluetooth. That means that the bluetooth was on all day, I was downloading and installing all day long. I have to say that I am shocked. It is about 12 hours later and there is still over 50% battery left. I had to recharge my Acer once during all of this time.

So, compared to what I am used to (which is about 2-4 hours of work on a tablet before recharging, including no location turned on) this tablet is dreamy for me. The battery is way beyond what I am used to with the Acer, so I am very happy.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I will update as I find things to tell you about, but I wanted to start off with the basics as that is what I was looking for when I was trying to decide if I should get this tablet or not. I still do not find tablets to be useful for all of my work, but they are great for smaller web surfing, quick look ups, apps for certain things and of course games and skype. As for the keyboard and typing, it is not really practical at least for me to use this for heavier loads of work- desktop or laptop are best suited for that.

Is it worth the price? At $300 it is a very powerful device with a screen that blows anything else I have seen out of the water. The colors are a feast for the eyes, the clarity is crisp, and the smooth operation is delightful. If you really enjoy having a tablet you can depend on, I would say that this fits the bill.

Could you do with something less expensive? Yes. But you might have more frustration with that lower price tag. The set up of this tablet is easy to work with, great operation and having two windows open at the same time is delightful. I am very happy with this and despite my misgivings after reading so many reviews with disappointment in them I can say at this point, I am very very glad that I went ahead and got it. It is a really great tablet.

I stayed in a vacation home with a Roku 2 last summer, and it was great, but it also had to buffer a lot. We also have three game consoles that have streaming video apps, and they buffer, too. I think the Fire's secret may be its wifi card. I am sure that, at some point, my ISP will find a way to slow it down.

So, yeah, I am giving the Fire TV four stars for doing exactly what I need it to do. I had come to Amazon to get another Chromecast, but I saw this and thought it would probably be better suited to what I need in my bedroom (I need my husband to be able to watch a tv show without my help - he is completely tech-challenged and cannot work the Dish remote - too many buttons).

The reason it doesn't get five stars is that there aren't yet enough content apps. There is a manga channel, a documentary channel, an art house channel, along with Crackle and Flixter and Plex (Plex is a for pay service that lets you stream your home content). There is plenty to watch if you are a Prime member (I am - and I appreciated having that already set up on my Fire TV - Thank you, Amazon!) I am also a Dish subscriber, with HBO and a Hopper. I have apps for those directly on some of my devices. I can get them on the internet on the tbs I have hooked up to computers. I can even blast them over to my Chromecast from my tablets. But they aren't on Fire TV, and none of my tablets will screencast to Fire TV. Soon as they are, this is a five star device for me.

I read in Entertainment Weekly that HBO and Amazon Prime have come to an understanding that will make lots and lots of HBO shows available through prime, which will also make them available through Fire TV. For the ones that are not, HBOGO will have an app for this. Between that news and my son's enjoyment of an eight dollar (as opposed to 40 to 60 dollars) platformed on this thing, I am adding a star.

This auxiliary lens support is superb and works extraordinarily well.

If you want to put a long lens on your DSLR or Panasonic GH4, and you have a 15mm rod system, this is indispensable if you want to achieve a solid rig, especially during focusing or zooming.

Pros:
- Solid machined aluminum with hard black anodizing
- No parts can escape; it's cleverly assembled as a unit
- Thin profile (about 5/16" thin); it fits under the lens, supports and doesn't take too much room
- Quick disconnect from the 60mm-spaced 15mm rods, but attaches firmly
- Adjustable height
- Locking knobs are easily accessible, not under the lens; no tools or pesky allen wrench required
- One knob locks the device to the rods, the other locks height
- The height locking knob bites into a machined groove so as the aluminum becomes nicked by the lock, it still allows for smooth movement up and down. This is good engineering.
- The brilliantly-designed rubber hold-down strap is about 3/8" wide and adjusts to any size up to my 4-3/8" diameter [[ASIN:B004JHY5LU Rokinon 800M-B-AI 800mm F8.0 Mirror Lens for Nikon (Black)]]...which really needs this support at that focal length.
- Mounts faster under the lens than fiddling with a bridge and 1/4-20 bolt, should the lens have an aux tripod shoe, which many lenses do not. Much faster to mount my 70-200mm Nikon lens that if I bolt it down via its tripod foot.
- Works with any lens as long as there is a part of the lens that doesn't rotate that you can wrap the rubber strap over; you obviously cannot strap this to the focus or zoom rings
- Is amazingly stable; the rubber strap really holds, even though it's flexible
- Goes on and off in a flash
- Stores compactly
- Light weight and simple

Cons:
- The rubber strap, I fear, will only last so long, and will eventually rot or harden and crack. It is a molded strap that is attached to the device at one end via a hinge pin that doesn't appear to be removable. Even then, I'm sure a small bungee or something else could be pressed into duty. And if I keep it sealed in a ziplock poly bag away from UV and ozone, it should last years and years. Also, don't keep it under tension; let the rubber relax between jobs.

- A bit pricy in absolute terms, but in relative terms compared to other supports I shopped for out there, this is a bargain. Some are hundreds of dollars. And Amazon got it here in two days.

Bottom line, this firms up the lens, especially when equipped with a follow focus unit, eases downward pressure on the camera flange and allows steady tracking when using a good tripod and head.

Couldn't be happier.

This sleeping bag is designed to keep you warm in temperatures as low as 14 degrees Fahrenheit, yet still be comfortable to sleep in without becoming too hot at temperatures up to 50 degrees, so it's a cold weather bag not intended for 0 degrees or below. I didn't have any trouble rolling it back up and getting it back into it's case when we finished with it either. Just be sure to fold the bag over lengthwise then roll from feet towards the head compressing as you go, and then work the edge of the bag around the bag before starting to pull it up over the bag.

This bag feels very comfortable without feeling too hot inside, but I can't say how well it would do in under 30 degree temperatures since we had no way to test that. Here in South Texas this sleeping bag will be perfectly adequate for the weather we get however, and the inflatable travel pillow that comes with it is a nice touch. These binoculars are all about quality in the largest field of view. If you want to see a wide expanse of nature or the heavens downrange from your position, these are the way to go. I got them specifically to frame smaller constellations and asterisms, the detail of which can be further examined with a scope. They help tremendously to put the object in the scope into context. Ordinarily, observing half a degree of field tends to abstract objects almost entirely from their surrounding. Since it's not practical to really "zoom" in using a single optical instrument, using these in combination with something of higher power is ideal. Don't get me wrong, I do have a zoom on the scope... it zooms from 25x to 50x -- amazing but you have to understand that this is a field of view of 2.4 to 1.5 degrees -- essentially like looking through a pipe to a drinkstraw. These Nikons however, show over 9 degrees field of view -- something which is unsurpassed in the highest-end binocular out there.

There are compromises necessitated by the optical principles used to make these function. They do not have a very flat field of view, meaning objects in the center of the field (circle) can be focused, but objects nearer the edge of the field are out of focus. This is because the focused field is curved not flat. This problem is also evident in most 10x50's for example. It's less of a problem in good quality 8x42's like Nikon's Monarch for example, and obviously the high end Swarovski, Leica, Zeiss etc. This problem matters more when you have a narrow field and highly magnified image where the subject tends to fill the field of view. It matters less when the subject is focused in the center of the field and the background surrounding it is slightly out of focus.

Still, even if you pay the biggest bucks for bright, flat, and sharp images from the top of the line binoculars, you'll still only see about 8 degrees true field of view, whereas these give you over 9 degrees. Furthermore, they give an apparent field of view of over 59 degrees, rivaling the top-of-the-line binoculars.

If you're looking for a handy, all-purpose binocular, the roof-prism 8x42's are proven to be far more popular for a number of good reasons (more compact, more magnification while not yet needing a tripod or IS like 10x does, more competition and choices etc.) But if you're looking for the best field of view with high quality optics, this is it, and fortunately it comes at a very reasonable cost. I don't know what other 7x35's are out there, but I can tell you this is far better than Celestron or Bushnell.

If you are looking at this then you are probably also looking at the KBP V60, which costs virtually the same. The only reason to get that board is you prefer illumination, ABS keycaps, don't need the programmability, and prefer a lighter board. I also purchased the V60 and am waiting for it to be delivered. I want to make sure that I am making the right choice.

Other boards to consider are the Choc Mini, although this is a lower class board, it may meet your needs. There is the Ducky Mini which has an aluminum bezel which makes it larger which kind of defeats the purpose of the 60% board IMHO. There is the Tex Beetle. These are all at a similar price point and similar layout. I will post back after I have had the V60 for a few days. Who knows, maybe I will actually prefer it. I'm not 100% sure I like the PBT keycaps as they feel like typing on cubes of concrete, although I would be in the minority. Also worth mentioning is that the space bar kind of creaks when it is depressed. I'm not sure if it is the stabilizer, spring, or defect, but it is mildly annoying. (One more thing I want to mention is that my favorite mechanical keyboard ever is the Cherry MX Board 3.0. It is more of an economy board, but the keystrokes are the smoothest, the board is quieter, and it has great low profile keys which really do make typing smoother. I don't know why these have not caught on).

Edit: I wan to add that have since purchsed the Poker 3 LED. It gives typing a different feel. In comparison, the PBT keycaps make the keystrokes feel stiff and mushy. I actually prefer the LED version with the ABS. They are fairly high quality, not the crap you get on a typical Dell keyboard. My preference for ABS goes against the grain as most prefer PBT, but this is all subjective.

I have worked with K&F Concept filters in the past and generally had good experiences with them. They're good, mid-range quality filters at (usually) a budget price. I haven't worked with any black diffusion filters prior to this one so I have no basis against which to compare, but so far it seems to work as designed and seems to be made very well.

In a nutshell, this type of filter softens light a bit, causing some gentle halos around light sources, without impacting image sharpness or detail. Where I have seen the most noticeable impact is in images where there otherwise would be a lot of shadows and contrast; instead of stark contrast and strong shadows, the filter has the effect of brightening up the shadows somewhat and creating smoother color gradients. Sure, this can be done in software after the fact, but it is a lot easier to do this at the time the image is taken and it certainly is a lot less work.

The filter is very easy to install. This is my first magnetic filter and it is as easy to attach to my camera as I could have hoped. The threaded ring attaches to the lens in the same manner as a step ring or another filter, and the filter itself just snaps securely into place due to the magnetics. Removing the filter is just as simple, especially if you choose to leave the magnetic ring in place on the lens.

The assembly seems to be well made. I have had filters in the past that have been poorly constructed and rattle in the frames when shaken, or have been mildly blemished, or just felt cheap. This filter has none of those issues and appears to be well made.

This is a nice black diffusion filter. It's easy to install and use, and it just works. I will be using it more in the coming weeks.
Easy to use and won't rattle. I also use these to attach filter screens and they're much simpler to remove and clean than with screws.

I think I'll just do a simple pro and con list for this one.

Pros:

+ It starts up fast when switched on and immediately reconnects to the last Bluetooth device selected.

+ The ability to store multiple device profiles and switch between them with the press of a button is awesome, and it saves a lot of time over having to open the Bluetooth settings on each device to reconnect.

+ And of course it has a 2.4g wireless USB dongle, so you can use it with things that don't have Bluetooth or which require a stronger wireless signal.

+ There are visible-yet-unobtrusive lights on the top that allow you to tell at a glance which device pairing you have selected.

+ The shape of the mouse fits my hand perfectly and is very comfortable.

+ The scroll wheel is easy to grip and roll back and forth. It has a very satisfying sort of "bump" feeling as it rotates from one position to another, whereas some wheels just turn freely, leaving you little control over how much you're actually scrolling. And most importantly, the wheel doesn't rock side-to-side like those ones that supposedly allow you to scroll left and right but never seem to work except by accident when you don't want them to.

+ There's no branding that I can identify on the packaging, the instructions, nor on the mouse itself. I see this as a pro because well, frankly, a lot of these random brand names are weird and bother me (though admittedly, I did once buy a product on Amazon primarily because the brand name was BULLETFACE *cue electric guitar solo*).

+ I really appreciate how every feature on this mouse serves a purpose. There are no dumb shapes or graphics added just to make it look "cool". It's cool enough as it is.

+ It's great that it has a built-in rechargeable battery and a USB-C port on the front so that I can charge it wherever I can charge my phone. But because there's no battery access door, the dongle rests in a recess on the underside of the mouse and is held in by a really strong magnet. That's better than other attachment methods I've seen where the dongle either snaps in with plastic clips or press-fits into a slot, as those will both wear out and fail eventually, where a magnet will not.

Cons:

- The ball feels a bit loose and rattle-y in its socket. It's not an issue when the mouse is on a level surface, but if you're carrying it around or trying to use it on the arm of a sofa, it can wiggle a bit, which feels weird.

- All but the lowest DPI setting is way too fast for anything I can imagine doing, but maybe I'm just not used to it yet. (Update: I guess I wasn't used to it. I've since moved up to the middle DPI setting now that I've gotten better at making fine movements)

- This may not be a con for some people, but the dongle really, really stays put in a USB port, to the point I was afraid I'd need pliers to get it out (though I managed to do so without them).

- Update: I thought of one more con. It's a shame I can't re-bind the little forward and back buttons on the far left to something more useful, like shift or ctrl-z.

Conclusion:

I'm currently very satisfied with my purchase, and I expect to get a lot of use out of this mouse for years to come. The best thing I can do to thank the manufacturer and seller for making a great product at a great price is to leave my honest feedback to help others find the product, so that's exactly what I've done. Oh, and I swyped (typed via path input) this entire review on my phone's on-screen keyboard using the very trackball I'm reviewing, if that gives you an idea of how comfortable and accurate it is to operate.

I have gotten more into creative photography and I have enjoyed playing with lens filters like these. I have worked with star filters in the past and I thought it might be fun to experiment with this light streak filter as well. So far I have no complaints, though it is the type of filter that should be used sparingly.

This is a gold streak filter that works in the same way as star filters, only it channels light in a straight line across the frame instead of in multiple directions. That is, it can make lights look smeared as if swept from one direction in a straight line. The color of the filter lines alters the light slightly and it has a mildly warming effect.

Some thought went into this filter and it allows for turning the filter (similar to a CPL) so that it can channel light in any single direction.

As with any filter like this, it should be used sparingly. It is possible to have too much of a good thing and as such this can easily be overdone. When used properly and used infrequently it can make some very striking and impactful photos.

It seems to be well made. There are no hitches in the turn when making directional adjustments, and the glass does not rattle loosely in the metal frame. I have found no damage to the glass or metal right out of the package either.

One question that might come up is, why should you use this kind of filter then it is easy to do the same thing in software? The answer is straightforward - it's fun!

This is very much a fun and useful filter but it is a special-use thing that should be used with some restraint. It seems to be well made and it does generate the desired effects. It is not particularly expensive either which is a plus.

I purchased this for two specific reasons: (1) safety because too many accidents are caused by drivers with a phone to their ear, and (2) I love music and my Droid X has become my MP3 player (among other things as well as a phone.

Installation was a snap, although I did have to read the directions, which were clear and easy to follow. In less than 5 minutes after removing it from the packaging I was listening to music through my car radio!

This device comes with a fairly short USB charging cable that connects to a port on the head. The length made it inconvenient, and it was pretty flimsy too, failing after about three months. I added a [[ASIN:B0042X8XQO PowerLine 90310 Auto Socket Splitter with USB Power Port]] (which cleared my console in my 2008 Mazda 3 with the GOgroove and [[ASIN:B000S5Q9CA Motorola Vehicle Power Adapter micro-USB Rapid Rate Charger]] plugged in), and the combination, while unwieldy, has worked perfectly ever since.

Music and calls are reasonably clear. I do have to turn my radio volume up when a call comes in, but that may be an issue with my phone and not the GOgroove. And, like a hands-free system should work, when there is an incoming call or you wish to make an outgoing one, the MP3 player feature in my Droid X pauses the music until I am finished using the phone. After calls are terminated any paused music will automatically resume.

For long trips where you pass through areas with radio stations, your clear signal set in one location may start to degrade and you will notice static. That is caused by you coming into the range of a strong FM signal that is competing with the one you selected. You will need to seek and switch to a new frequency when that happens. For example, if I am traveling from, say, Ormond Beach, FL to Jacksonville, FL, I will need to change my frequency twice going up and twice again returning. It's the nature of any such device and there is nothing that can be designed into the GOgroove to fix it - at least not at the price point at which this device is selling.

I've had friends connect to it with their iPhones, and it works without a hitch. The icing on the cake is the GOgroove remains paired with my Droid X, and automatically connects to it as soon as I start my car if I am playing music. This is a convenient feature that I wish my [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]] that is connected to my home stereo had - I have to manually connect to that device anytime I want to use it.

Overall I am thrilled with my GOgroove and if it dies I would not hesitate to purchase another. In fact, I am considering purchasing a spare anyway because I spend a lot of time in my car and life without this wonderful gizmo would not be the same.

Prior to Alesis coming up with this and its larger sibling, the [[ASIN:B005NIVLX4 Alesis Mic Tube Duo Stereo Tube Microphone Preamplifier]], I was sold on the venerable [[ASIN:B0002D0KG4 PreSonus Tubepre Single-Channel Vacuum Tube Mic Pre]] as the "gold standard" in lower end tube microphone tube amps. I personally think this and the 2-channel model that Alesis offers are game changers, mainly because the features and reliability are on par with the PreSonus competing products, and the price point is significantly less. In other words, bang for your buck.

Before rushing out and getting one of these (or its larger sibling - or even the competing PreSonus), make sure you need it. I have found that on a reasonably decent PA system this product makes a dramatic difference with the older technology mics like [[ASIN:B000CZ0R3S Shure SM57 Microphone]] and the [[ASIN:B000CZ0R42 Shure SM58-LC Cardioid Vocal Microphone without Cable]], or the lower end SM58 clones that are bundled with PA systems and otherwise flood the market (the [[ASIN:B00009W40D NADY SP-4C Dynamic Microphone]] comes to mind). On the other hand, not only have I found that these tube pre-amps not very useful with more modern design microphones like the [[ASIN:B002SQJL9U Blue Microphones enCORE 100 Studio-Grade Dynamic Performance Microphone]], the [[ASIN:B00006I5R7 Sennheiser E835 Dynamic Cardioid Microphone]], etc. In fact, with the more modern designed microphones, which run much hotter in signal, a pre-amp in a live PA needs to have the gain turned to the lowest level in many cases or feedback becomes a problem.

If you do need one of these devices, I recommend - unless your budget is severely limited - that you consider the [[ASIN:B005NIVLX4 Alesis Mic Tube Duo Stereo Tube Microphone Preamplifier]] instead. The reason is for a slight increase in price you get an extra channel that you may not need now, but may find to be a requirement in the future.
I hear absolutely nothing when these are in; they cancel out all other noise, and the volume goes way higher than I need. These are good to get.

I was able to do a direct comparison between this and the SwissGear SA1908 ScanSmart Backpack. And it turns out that deciding which pack to grab on the way out is surprisingly one of the hardest decisions one could have to make. Both packs are obviously of the best quality with a similar nylon shell, strong stitching, and smooth zippers. Both are designed to fit 17" laptops and have similar interior volumes, and yet the features vary widely. Let's have a look at key points:

-The Targus is perfect for a user carrying a laptop and a tablet and/or Kindle. In front of the laptop compartment is a soft fabric lined pocket to hold a tablet against the laptop and protect the screen from scratches. The very front pocket is also soft with a piece of padding that fits the newest Kindle nicely.

-The SwissGear may be better for carrying just a laptop or two laptops. It has the ScanSmart feature, which is great when TSA allows it to work (sometimes they make you remove your computer anyway, either out of ignorance or their suspicion that you packed incorrectly for it to work - that makes it easier just to remove it sometimes rather than risk a fight with them). And I often store a second laptop in the ScanSmart opening.

-I love that on the Targus, the zipper pulls for the main compartment and the two side compartments can be placed between the bag and your back, thwarting casual thieves. As an extremely paranoid person, this gives extra peace of mind. For that matter, I really like the unique design of these pockets. The side pockets can be really useful, and the big compartment can be accessed from a larger opening. But that uniqueness comes at a cost...

-...and that cost is the looks. I didn't like the looks on the picture, but then it grew on me. In person, I don't really like it that much, but it might be growing on me. I guess the tradeoff is simple: you get a very unique design that works great and you get some serious padding for your electronics and some extra comfortable straps, but that all equals a slightly awkward looking pack. It's not too bad, but I think an accent color would go a long way. In contrast, the SwissGear under observation is quite beautiful and more traditional, yet not as padded or protected.

-The Targus came in a very thin box. It has a semi-rigid pad on the bottom that can fold up to flatten it out or fold down and attach with velcro to add some structure to the main compartment. This is also a very smart feature.

-The SwissGear has a phone/MP3 player holder with earphone exit, for those interested. That's not the best one I've ever seen though, as it is only a hanging cradle for the device.

-The Targus has more padding, while the SwissGear has a better airflow system for your back.

Conclusion: I really love both of these backpacks, and I'm surprised how different two top notch backpacks can be. I can see how the designers have to pick and choose the features they want to incorporate, because you really just can't have it all without making the pack bigger, and I wouldn't want that. They both deserve five stars, absolutely. The Targus strikes me as the pack for someone serious about the transportation and protection of their electronics, or anyone else who is intrigued to try this unique, excellent design.

Update: A good pencil sleeve to use with this case after stretching it out a bit with a crayola dry erase marker is the Hydream Silicone Case for Apple Pencil Holder Sleeve Skin Pocket Cover Accessories for iPad Pro 9.7/10.5/12.9, Cute Soft Grip Pouch with Charging Cap Holder and 2 Protective Nib Covers.

TL:DR - a fantastic case and looks amazing with a screen protector on the device. Does not interfere with screen protectors at all. Great utility and angle options. Looks good on the fridge too. If you don't mind the case feeling a bit awkward to hold when looking at things in portrait and the fact that your Pencil Sleeve options are limited due to the super tight elastic (I used a crayola dry eraser to stretch mine and now the fit perfect) this is the case for you.

Pros:
8 Adjustment points
The packaging and info included on the company
The quality
The looks (at least in black for me)
The pencil sleeve built in
The wake/sleep utility
Solid positions minus the last one if you're really pretty on it. Like heavy handed drawing hard.

Cons:
The tablet is hard to hold in portrait especially if the pencil is in the case
I know the 2018 Pro model had yet to be released when this case was made, but I wish the placement of the Pencil sleeve was in a better location or allowed enough space for a wider variety of pencil sleeves. It makes me worry that it sticks out a little from the case. Kinda wish it was on the top or had a similar elastic sleeve loop on the top where an Apple Pencil 2 would sit magnetically. More or a nitpick though.
The tightness of the sleeve out of the box! This was very annoying, but another nitpick since I can always stretch it out.
A little awkward to use the rear-facing camera since when holding with the front panel touching the back of the case it covers the camera completely. Even when in landscape you have to tilt it high enough to free your view.

Quality of Life Cons: (basically super nitpicks. Feel free to ignore. The case is great!)
Would have been nice if they added another small sleeve near the rear pencil sleeve for the small charging Pencil dongle. It looks like there is enough room in the back.
Like the little indents where the power and volume buttons are located I'd have liked to see a little notch above the charging port center of the charging port. Why? Because I often find myself inserting the connector low of the actual charging port and a little notch where the middle would generally be would have been a nice touch or at least some more material to alleviate confusion on the port's location. If you look at the charging port with the case on you'll see what I mean, there is a little lip which can make it confusing on what I'm inserting the plug into (done this a lot lately, but getting better at it).
A somewhat more rigid hinge on the panel that covers the screen. Why? It can get really floppy when holding it in portrait mode and a slightly more rigid hinge kind of like the surface pro keyboard cover would have been nice. The panel itself is solid but the material connecting it to the case can be a little floppy.
